export async function runHourly(triggeredById?: string): Promise<JobResult[]> {
  const results: JobResult[] = [];

  results.push(await run("erp-alerts", erpAlertsStep, triggeredById));
  results.push(await run("erp-inbox", erpInboxStep, triggeredById));

  results.push(await run("mbos-hourly", mbosHourly, triggeredById));

  // The Top customers report has its own 10:00 IST cron line on the 1st. This
  // is the net under it: a droplet whose crontab predates that line still
  // gets the month's report within the hour, and on every other hour it is
  // one indexed lookup that finds the report already there.
  results.push(await run("top-customers-report", topCustomersReportStep, triggeredById));

  // The founder's WhatsApp rules. The pass checks the sending window itself
  // (10 am–1 pm IST unless the founder changed it) and returns at once
  // outside it, so running every hour costs nothing between checks.
  results.push(
    await run("whatsapp-automation", async () => {
      const { runAutomation } = await import("./services/whatsapp-automation-service");
      const r = await runAutomation({ source: "schedule" });
      return {
        recordsAffected: r.sent,
        detail: `${r.sent} sent, ${r.wouldSend} would send — ${r.note}`,
      };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  results.push(
    await run("sweep-unconfirmed", async () => {
      const { swept, autoConfirmed } = await sweepUnconfirmed();
      return {
        recordsAffected: swept,
        detail: `${swept} unconfirmed copies, ${autoConfirmed} auto-confirmed`,
      };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  // Delivered and read, read back from Wati's history for the last week —
  // the webhook has not been bringing them (see lib/wati-receipts.ts).
  results.push(
    await run("whatsapp-receipts", async () => {
      const { refreshReceipts } = await import("./services/whatsapp-receipts-service");
      const r = await refreshReceipts({ days: 7 });
      return {
        recordsAffected: r.updated,
        detail: `${r.updated} ticks moved across ${r.numbers} numbers${r.errors ? `, ${r.errors} numbers Wati did not answer for` : ""}`,
      };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  // A file a customer sent that arrived without its path — found in Wati's
  // history, so the chat can show it. Two days back; by hand reads everything.
  results.push(await runReplyMedia(triggeredById, 2));

  results.push(
    await run("escalate-complaint-sla", async () => {
      const breached = await db
        .select({ id: complaints.id, customerId: complaints.customerId })
        .from(complaints)
        .where(
          and(
            lt(complaints.slaDueAt, new Date()),
            isNull(complaints.resolvedAt),
            isNull(complaints.slaEscalatedAt),
          ),
        );

      if (breached.length) {
        const managers = await db
          .select({ id: users.id })
          .from(users)
          .where(sql`${users.role} in ('manager','admin')`);

        for (const c of breached) {
          await db
            .update(complaints)
            .set({ slaEscalatedAt: new Date() })
            .where(eq(complaints.id, c.id));
          for (const m of managers) {
            await notifyUsers([
              {
                userId: m.id,
                title: "Complaint past its SLA",
                body: "A complaint has passed its resolution deadline and needs attention.",
                kind: "danger",
                href: "/crm/complaints",
              },
            ]);
          }
        }
      }
      return {
        recordsAffected: breached.length,
        detail: `${breached.length} complaints escalated`,
      };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  /*
   * THE SALESMAN SCORE, THIS MONTH ONLY — and it was missing entirely.
   *
   * The handset reads the cache rather than deriving anything, so until this
   * ran the only thing that moved a figure on a salesman's phone was the
   * NIGHTLY pass: a target published at ten in the morning, or three orders
   * taken before lunch, reached him the next day.
   *
   * THIS MONTH AND NOT THE PREVIOUS ONE. The nightly rebuilds both, because a
   * receipt confirmed on the 2nd of September is usually August's collection
   * and a closed month must not freeze half-finished. Inside a working day
   * that correction can wait, and doing it twenty-four times over is a pass of
   * the whole company's order book to move a figure nobody is being judged on
   * any more.
   *
   * It needs nothing recomputed before it, unlike in the nightly: every figure
   * it reads — orders, receipts, bills, tasks — comes off the ledger itself
   * rather than off a derived cache, so there is no ordering to get wrong.
   */
  results.push(
    await run("recompute-performance", async () => {
      const day = await today();
      const period = day.slice(0, 7);
      const { people } = await recomputeSalesPerformance(period, day);
      return { recordsAffected: people, detail: `${people} scored for ${period}` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  return results;
}

export async function runNightly(triggeredById?: string): Promise<JobResult[]> {
  const day = await today();
  const results: JobResult[] = [];

  /* The field app's nightly tidy-up rides the same schedule as the CRM's.
     One cron, one place to look when something did not run. */
  results.push(await run("mbos-nightly", mbosNightly, triggeredById));

  /* HRMS's monthly paid-leave credit. Nightly rather than on the 1st: the
     partial unique index makes every run after the first a no-op, and a
     night the cron missed is caught the next night. */
  results.push(
    await run("hrms-leave-credit", async () => {
      const { runMonthlyLeaveCredit } = await import("./hrms/jobs");
      const r = await runMonthlyLeaveCredit();
      return { recordsAffected: r.created, detail: `${r.created} credit${r.created === 1 ? "" : "s"} written` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  /* The ERP's alert pass, and the owner's paragraph built from it (AI-4). */
  results.push(await run("erp-alerts", erpAlertsStep, triggeredById));
  results.push(
    await run("erp-digest", async () => {
      const { writeErpDigest } = await import("./erp/digest");
      const r = await writeErpDigest();
      return { recordsAffected: 1, detail: `${r.day} · written by ${r.servedBy}` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  /* This month's expense figures, frozen.
     Requirement 72's trend reads the snapshot rather than the ledger, so that
     a closed month reads the same on every load and correcting an old claim
     does not silently redraw a chart somebody made a decision from. Only the
     CURRENT month is written: a past month stops being overwritten the day it
     closes, which is what makes it correct without any job firing on exactly
     the right date. */
  results.push(
    await run("expense-month-snapshot", async () => {
      const { snapshotExpenseMonth } = await import(
        "@/lib/services/expense-roi-service"
      );
      const rows = await snapshotExpenseMonth(day.slice(0, 7));
      return {
        recordsAffected: rows,
        detail: `${day.slice(0, 7)}: ${rows} rows, one per salesman plus the company total`,
      };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  /* Where the goods went, from the tab that has always known and never said.
     Before the caches, because nothing downstream reads it yet — and after the
     reconcile that lands the rows it reads. */
  results.push(
    await run("link-delivery-parties", async () => {
      const { linkDeliveryParties } = await import(
        "@/lib/services/delivery-party-service"
      );
      const r = await linkDeliveryParties();
      return {
        recordsAffected: r.linked + r.cleared,
        detail: `${r.linked} linked, ${r.cleared} cleared, ${r.unresolved} unmatched names`,
      };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  /* Which shop each old-app row is, re-judged against today's book and the
     names people have decided — so a shop added since is linked, and nothing
     is ever linked on a close name. Cheap: an exact name is a map lookup. */
  results.push(
    await run("field-activity-shops", async () => {
      const c = await rematchFieldActivityCustomers();
      const p = await projectFieldActivityTimeline();
      return {
        recordsAffected: c.moved,
        detail: `${c.moved} rows changed · ${c.timelineRemoved} timeline entries removed · ${p.written} written`,
      };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  results.push(
    await run("recompute-cycles", async () => {
      const n = await recomputeAllBuyingCycles();
      // Customers whose cycle MOVED. The whole book is read every pass and
      // almost none of it changes between two passes an hour apart, so a
      // figure near zero here is the pass working rather than the pass idling.
      return { recordsAffected: n, detail: `${n} customers changed` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  /*
   * The sales manager seat, kept in step with the org chart — for every
   * customer nobody has ever decided this on. A person's own pick, made
   * through `assignSalesManager`, is off limits here exactly the way a
   * reassignment is off limits to `recomputeSalesPeople` above it.
   */
  results.push(
    await run("recompute-sales-managers", async () => {
      const n = await recomputeSalesManagers();
      return { recordsAffected: n, detail: `${n} customers updated` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  /*
   * The person Mahek designates to approve a lead its Sales Manager raised
   * herself, seated on each one so they can see it. After the pass above, which
   * may have just seated the Sales Manager. Does nothing until somebody is
   * designated on the Settings screen.
   */
  results.push(
    await run("self-raised-verifier-seats", async () => {
      const { ensureSelfRaisedVerifierSeats } = await import("./services/self-raised-verifier-service");
      const n = await ensureSelfRaisedVerifierSeats();
      return { recordsAffected: n, detail: `${n} leads seated` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  /*
   * Where each shop is, for every account the location review never saw —
   * matched from the sheet's own text against the reviewed tree, so a shop
   * created today can be filtered by state, district, city and area tomorrow.
   * A reviewed or hand-picked place is never touched.
   */
  results.push(
    await run("resolve-typed-places", async () => {
      const out = await resolveTypedPlaces();
      await refreshPlaceCounts();
      return { recordsAffected: out.considered, detail: out.detail };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  results.push(
    await run("recompute-inactivity", async () => {
      const n = await recomputeInactivity();
      return { recordsAffected: n, detail: `${n} on the watch` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  results.push(
    await run("recompute-followups", async () => {
      await recomputeBillStatuses();
      await recomputeAllOutstanding();
      const n = await recomputeAllFollowUpStates();
      return { recordsAffected: n, detail: `${n} customers evaluated` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  // §4.2 — an abandoned form leaves files belonging to nothing. Nothing else
  // will ever reclaim them, so the sweep is part of the subsystem rather than
  // a tidy-up somebody remembers to run.
  results.push(
    await run("sweep-orphan-attachments", async () => {
      const { swept } = await sweepOrphans();
      return { recordsAffected: swept, detail: `${swept} unbound files removed` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  results.push(
    await run("recompute-slow-payers", async () => {
      const n = await recomputeSlowPayers();
      return { recordsAffected: n, detail: `${n} customers evaluated` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  // After the recomputes, never before: the snapshot has to record the list as
  // it will actually be read today, and the recomputes are what decide who is
  // on it.
  results.push(
    await run("snapshot-queue", async () => {
      const n = await snapshotQueue(day);
      return { recordsAffected: n, detail: `${n} rows recorded for ${day}` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  /*
   * Where every customer stands, written over this month's row.
   *
   * AFTER the cycle and outstanding recomputes, because the band is measured
   * against the customer's own cycle and reading it first would snapshot last
   * night's rhythm. It is the only thing in this job that is not a cache: a
   * past month's row is never rewritten, because it is the only surviving
   * record of where somebody stood then, and "how many customers came back"
   * has no answer without it.
   */
  results.push(
    await run("snapshot-customer-health", async () => {
      const { customers, period } = await snapshotCustomerHealth(day);
      return { recordsAffected: customers, detail: `${customers} banded for ${period}` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  /*
   * The salesman score, AFTER the money recomputes above.
   *
   * Order matters: collection reads confirmed receipts and outstanding has
   * just been rebuilt, so scoring first would grade everybody against
   * yesterday's ledger. Both the current month and the previous one are
   * rebuilt — a receipt confirmed on the 2nd of September is usually August's
   * collection, and a month that stopped being recomputed the moment it ended
   * would freeze half-finished.
   */
  results.push(
    await run("recompute-performance", async () => {
      const period = day.slice(0, 7);
      const previous = addMonths(period, -1);
      const now = await recomputeSalesPerformance(period, day);
      const then = await recomputeSalesPerformance(previous, day);
      return {
        recordsAffected: now.people + then.people,
        detail: `${now.people} scored for ${period}, ${then.people} for ${previous}`,
      };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  // Only on the first of the month, but harmless to call any day: it seeds
  // only customers without a target.
  if (day.endsWith("-01")) {
    results.push(
      await run("seed-targets", async () => {
        const n = await seedMonthlyTargets();
        return { recordsAffected: n, detail: `${n} default targets seeded` };
      }, triggeredById),
    );

    // Same idempotence: only a person with no target at all for the new
    // period gets one, copied from last month's published figures.
    results.push(
      await run("copy-forward-sales-targets", async () => {
        const n = await copyForwardSalesTargets();
        return { recordsAffected: n, detail: `${n} sales targets carried forward` };
      }, triggeredById),
    );
  }

  /*
   * The day that just ended, archived — LAST, deliberately. Every step above
   * this one feeds the Call Log, targets or the collections worklist, and
   * `run` re-throws on failure: a broken step stops everything after it in
   * this same list. Archiving a report must never be the thing that costs a
   * telecaller tomorrow's queue.
   *
   * `submitEod` already writes a real, finalised report the moment a
   * telecaller presses Submit; this is the safety net for whoever did not —
   * a zero-activity day must still produce a report, never silence. `day` is
   * the day about to start (`today()` has already stepped past the boundary
   * by the time this runs), so the day being archived is the one before it.
   *
   * `runDayBoundary` carries the same call for anybody who wants to trigger
   * it by hand at a different hour; `autoGenerateEodReports` never
   * overwrites a report that already exists, submitted or auto-generated by
   * an earlier pass, so the two cannot double-write.
   */
  results.push(
    await run("auto-eod", async () => {
      const yesterday = addDays(day, -1);
      const n = await autoGenerateEodReports(yesterday);
      return { recordsAffected: n, detail: `${n} reports generated for ${yesterday}` };
    }, triggeredById),
  );

  /* The call assistant's classifier, relearned from today's logged calls.
     Last, and allowed to fail on its own: a vote the assistant can do without
     for a day must never cost the caches above it. */
  try {
    results.push(await runCallIntelTraining(triggeredById));
  } catch (e) {
    console.error("Nightly: call assistant training failed:", e instanceof Error ? e.message : e);
  }

  return results;
}

function s3Config() {
  /*
   * The credentials this deployment ALREADY has.
   *
   * `R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID`, `R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` and `R2_ENDPOINT` are set for
   * the offsite database backups (`deploy/backup.sh`). Attachments are the
   * same account and the same token, so turning this on is ONE new variable —
   * the bucket — rather than a second copy of a credential that then has to be
   * rotated in two places and will not be.
   *
   * `S3_*` overrides all of it, for a deployment on something that is not R2.
   */
  const s3Bucket = process.env.S3_BUCKET;
  const usingS3 = Boolean(s3Bucket ?? process.env.S3_ENDPOINT);
  const endpoint = usingS3 ? process.env.S3_ENDPOINT : process.env.R2_ENDPOINT;
  const accessKeyId = usingS3 ? process.env.S3_ACCESS_KEY_ID : process.env.R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID;
  const secretAccessKey = usingS3
    ? process.env.S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY
    : process.env.R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY;
  if (!endpoint || !accessKeyId || !secretAccessKey) return null;

  const { host, bucketFromPath, protocol } = parseEndpoint(endpoint);
  /* The explicit variable wins, so somebody who has set both and changed their
     mind gets the one they last edited rather than the one buried in a URL. */
  const bucket = s3Bucket ?? process.env.R2_ATTACHMENTS_BUCKET ?? bucketFromPath;
  if (!bucket) return null;

  /*
   * **Never the backup bucket.** They are the same account and it is one
   * character to point at the wrong one — and the consequence is not a mess,
   * it is loss: the backup bucket has a retention policy that deletes old
   * objects, so every bill photograph would quietly disappear on a schedule
   * nobody associated with attachments. Refusing here means the store falls
   * back to Postgres, which is slow and correct, rather than to a bucket that
   * eats what it is given.
   */
  if (process.env.R2_BUCKET && bucket === process.env.R2_BUCKET) {
    console.error(
      "[storage] The attachments bucket is the same as R2_BUCKET, which is where database dumps go and which has a retention policy that deletes them. Attachments would be deleted on that schedule. Falling back to Postgres — give attachments their own bucket.",
    );
    return null;
  }

  return {
    bucket,
    host,
    protocol,
    /* R2 signs with the literal word `auto` and nothing else. A datacentre
       code here answers 403 and explains nothing. */
    region: process.env.S3_REGION ?? (usingS3 ? "us-east-1" : "auto"),
    accessKeyId,
    secretAccessKey,
  };
}

export async function createAttachment(input: {
  filename: string;
  bytes: Uint8Array;
  /** What the browser claimed. Recorded nowhere; used only to explain a refusal. */
  declaredType?: string;
  /**
   * A caller's own accepted list, checked against the SNIFFED type exactly as
   * the configured one is. The ERP's test video is the reason: an MP4 is
   * recognised by its `ftyp` box, which the sniffer names `audio/mp4`, and the
   * suite-wide list is images and PDFs. Passing it widens this one upload and
   * nothing else.
   */
  accepted?: string[];
  /** Store an MP4-family container as `video/mp4` rather than `audio/mp4`. */
  asVideo?: boolean;
  /**
   * A caller's own ceiling in megabytes, in place of `attachments.maxSizeMb`.
   * The Documents library is the reason: a catalogue is thirty megabytes where
   * a complaint photograph is three, and raising the shared setting for one
   * would raise it for the other. See `lib/publish-limits.ts`.
   */
  maxSizeMb?: number;
}): Promise<Result<{ id: string }>> {
  const ctx = await resolveScope();
  const config = await getConfig();

  const limitMb = input.maxSizeMb ?? config["attachments.maxSizeMb"];
  const maxBytes = limitMb * 1024 * 1024;
  if (input.bytes.byteLength > maxBytes) {
    const mb = (input.bytes.byteLength / (1024 * 1024)).toFixed(1);
    return err(
      `${input.filename} is ${mb} MB. The limit is ${limitMb} MB.`,
      "validation",
      [{ field: "file", message: "Too large." }],
    );
  }

  const sniffed = sniffContentType(input.bytes);
  const accepted = input.accepted ?? config["attachments.acceptedTypes"];
  const actual =
    input.asVideo && sniffed === "audio/mp4" ? "video/mp4" : input.asVideo && sniffed === "audio/webm" ? "video/webm" : sniffed;
  if (!actual || !(accepted.includes(actual) || (sniffed != null && accepted.includes(sniffed)))) {
    // Named precisely, because "invalid file" tells somebody nothing about
    // what to do next — and a renamed file is the interesting case.
    return err(
      actual
        ? `${input.filename} is a ${actual} file, which is not accepted here.`
        : `${input.filename} is not a JPG, PNG or PDF, whatever it is named.`,
      "validation",
      [{ field: "file", message: "Type not accepted." }],
    );
  }

  const attachmentId = id("att");
  try {
    const stored = await fileStorage.upload({
      key: `attachments/${attachmentId}`,
      body: input.bytes,
      contentType: actual,
    });

    await db.insert(attachments).values({
      id: attachmentId,
      filename: input.filename,
      storedRef: stored.ref,
      contentType: actual,
      sizeBytes: stored.sizeBytes,
      // Images are their own thumbnail: these are phone photographs under a
      // few megabytes, and a resize pipeline for that is machinery earning
      // nothing. PDFs show a file icon, per §4.2.
      thumbnailRef: actual.startsWith("image/") ? stored.ref : null,
      /* Requirement 47 — see the column's own note. Taken here because this is
         the only moment the bytes are in hand; hashing later would mean
         reading every file back out of the store. */
      contentHash: createHash("sha256").update(input.bytes).digest("hex"),
      status: "available",
      uploadedById: ctx.user.id,
    });

    return ok({ id: attachmentId }, `${input.filename} attached`);
  } catch (e) {
    // The row records the failure so the screen can say which file did not
    // make it, rather than the file simply not appearing.
    await db
      .insert(attachments)
      .values({
        id: attachmentId,
        filename: input.filename,
        storedRef: "",
        contentType: actual,
        sizeBytes: input.bytes.byteLength,
        status: "failed",
        uploadedById: ctx.user.id,
      })
      .catch(() => {});
    return err(
      `${input.filename} could not be stored. ${e instanceof Error ? e.message : ""}`.trim(),
      "conflict",
    );
  }
}

export function sniffContentType(bytes: Uint8Array): string | null {
  for (const sig of SIGNATURES) {
    if (sig.bytes.every((b, i) => bytes[i] === b)) return sig.type;
  }
  for (const sig of OFFSET_SIGNATURES) {
    if (sig.bytes.every((b, i) => bytes[sig.at + i] === b)) return sig.type;
  }
  return null;
}

export async function bindAttachments(
  attachmentIds: string[],
  parentType: ParentType,
  parentId: string,
): Promise<Result<{ bound: number; skipped: number }>> {
  if (!attachmentIds.length) return ok({ bound: 0, skipped: 0 });

  const limit = await limitFor(parentType);
  const existing = await db
    .select({ n: sql<number>`count(*)::int` })
    .from(attachments)
    .where(
      and(
        eq(attachments.parentType, parentType),
        eq(attachments.parentId, parentId),
        eq(attachments.status, "available"),
      ),
    );

  const room = Math.max(0, limit - Number(existing[0]?.n ?? 0));
  const toBind = attachmentIds.slice(0, room);
  const skipped = attachmentIds.length - toBind.length;

  if (toBind.length) {
    await db
      .update(attachments)
      .set({ parentType, parentId, updatedAt: new Date() })
      .where(
        and(inArray(attachments.id, toBind), isNull(attachments.parentId)),
      );
  }

  return ok({ bound: toBind.length, skipped });
}

const MBOS_PARENTS: Record<string, (typeof attachmentParentEnum.enumValues)[number]> = {
  attendance: "mbos_attendance",
  visit: "mbos_visit",
  expense: "mbos_expense",
  sample: "mbos_sample",
  task: "mbos_task",
  /* A shop front photographed while raising a lead. A lead IS a `customers`
     row, so `canRead` resolves this straight through the customer's scope. */
  lead: "mbos_lead",
  /* Not `mbos_payment`: a field collection is written into `payment_receipts`,
     the same table the CRM's own receipts use, so this is that parent and
     `canRead` resolves it through the customer exactly as it does for one
     captured at a desk. */
  payment: "payment_receipt",
  /*
   * THE ODOMETER PHOTOGRAPHS AND THE TICKET, which were being DELETED nightly.
   *
   * `mbos_travel_leg` has been in the attachment enum since the expense module
   * shipped and the handset has sent `parentType: 'travel_leg'` on every one of
   * these uploads — but this map never named it, so `storeMbosMedia` resolved
   * no parent and every file landed with `parent_id` null. `sweepOrphans`
   * selects exactly that past `attachments.orphanCleanupHours` and removes the
   * bytes: a meter photographed on Monday was gone on Tuesday. Until then it
   * was readable by its uploader alone, because `canRead` falls back to
   * "unbound and still the uploader's own" — so no approver had ever been able
   * to open one either.
   *
   * It is the same bug AGENTS.md already records for the whole MBOS media
   * subsystem, one parent type over, arriving with the module that was written
   * after the fix.
   */
  travel_leg: "mbos_travel_leg",
};

async function bindMbosMedia(
  attachmentId: string | null | undefined,
  parentType: (typeof attachmentParentEnum.enumValues)[number],
  parentId: string,
  /** Only the uploader's own file is bound — an id in a payload could name
      anybody's photograph, and binding it would move it under this record. */
  uploaderId: string,
): Promise<void> {
  if (!attachmentId) return;
  await db
    .update(attachments)
    .set({ parentType, parentId, updatedAt: new Date() })
    .where(and(eq(attachments.id, attachmentId), eq(attachments.uploadedById, uploaderId)))
    .catch(() => {});
}

export async function canRead(attachmentId: string): Promise<boolean> {
  const [row] = await db
    .select()
    .from(attachments)
    .where(eq(attachments.id, attachmentId));
  if (!row || row.status !== "available") return false;

  // Unbound and still the uploader's own: their form has not saved yet.
  if (!row.parentType || !row.parentId) {
    const ctx = await resolveScope();
    return row.uploadedById === ctx.user.id;
  }

  // Feedback is the one parent with no customer behind it, so it cannot be
  // answered by a customer's scope. The two sides of the thread may see the
  // screenshot and nobody else — the same rule that decides who may read the
  // words it was attached to, asked in one place.
  /* A price list document has no customer behind it either: whoever may read
   * price lists may open the file the list was read from, and nobody else.
   * Asked through the capability rather than the app, so the same rule answers
   * under /crm, /sales and the API. */
  /* ERP files belong to an ERP screen, never to a customer's scope: whoever may
     open the screen may open its files, and nobody else. */
  if (row.parentType.startsWith("erp_")) {
    const ctx = await resolveScope();
    const { canReadErpAttachment } = await import("@/lib/erp/attachments");
    return canReadErpAttachment(ctx.user.id, row.parentType, row.parentId);
  }

  /* HRMS files belong to an HRMS record, read under the screen it lives on. */
  if (row.parentType.startsWith("hrms_")) {
    const { canReadHrmsAttachment } = await import("@/lib/hrms/attachments");
    return canReadHrmsAttachment(row.parentType, row.parentId);
  }

  /* A factory job's photograph is evidence about the job: anybody holding the
     Factory app may open it, which is the team that loaded the truck and the
     Production Head who reviews it. */
  if (row.parentType === "factory_task") {
    const { listUserApps } = await import("@/lib/access");
    const ctx = await resolveScope();
    return (await listUserApps(ctx.user.id)).includes("factory");
  }

  /* A vendor's invoice has no customer behind it: whoever holds Accounts →
     Vendor payouts may open it, and nobody else. */
  if (row.parentType === "vendor_payout_invoice") {
    const ctx = await resolveScope();
    const { canReadPayoutInvoice } = await import("@/lib/services/vendor-payout-service");
    return canReadPayoutInvoice(ctx.user.id);
  }

  if (row.parentType === "price_list_document") {
    const ctx = await resolveScope();
    return canFor(ctx.user, "pricelist.read");
  }

  if (row.parentType === "feedback" || row.parentType === "feedback_message") {
    const ctx = await resolveScope();
    const feedbackId =
      row.parentType === "feedback"
        ? row.parentId
        : await feedbackBehindMessage(row.parentId);
    if (!feedbackId) return false;
    return canSeeFeedback(ctx.user, feedbackId);
  }

  /* The library, and the training beside it.
   *
   * A published document has no customer behind it unless somebody named one,
   * so it cannot be answered by a customer's scope either. Who may open it is
   * who the document was published TO: the roles on the row, and — where it
   * names a customer — that customer's scope on top. A withdrawn document is
   * refused, because withdrawing is how the office takes something back and it
   * would be no kind of withdrawal if the file stayed readable.
   *
   * Training is simpler: a course is published to the whole field or it is not
   * published. */
  if (row.parentType === "mbos_document") {
    return canReadDocument(row.parentId);
  }
  if (row.parentType === "mbos_course") {
    const [course] = await db
      .select({ active: mbosCourses.active })
      .from(mbosCourses)
      .where(eq(mbosCourses.id, row.parentId));
    return Boolean(course?.active);
  }

  /*
   * ATTENDANCE HAS NO CUSTOMER BEHIND IT, and every selfie was a 404.
   *
   * `customerBehind` below falls through to `calls` for any parent type it
   * does not name, so an attendance selfie's `parentId` — an
   * `mbos_attendance_days` id — was looked up in the calls table, found
   * nothing, and this returned false. Every check-in photograph ever taken was
   * refused to everybody, including the person in it and the manager it exists
   * for. It failed SHUT, which is the safe direction and exactly why it
   * survived: no screen displayed one, so there was nothing to notice it on.
   * It is the same bug AGENTS.md already records for the whole subsystem, one
   * parent type over, and it matters more now that the photograph is
   * mandatory: a proof nobody can open is not a proof.
   *
   * Who may see it: the salesman himself, and whoever can see his attendance —
   * which is the Sales Dashboard's own narrowing, `scopedToUsers`, so a
   * manager sees their own people and an admin sees everybody. Not "anyone
   * with the field app": a salesman must not be able to fetch a colleague's
   * photograph by id.
   */
  if (row.parentType === "mbos_attendance") {
    return canReadAttendanceSelfie(row.parentId);
  }

  /*
   * EVERY ODOMETER PHOTOGRAPH AND EVERY TICKET WAS A 404, to everybody.
   *
   * The same bug as the attendance selfie above, one parent type over, and it
   * arrived with the expense module: `mbos_travel_leg` had a place in the
   * enum, the media route filed files under it correctly, and nothing here
   * named it — so `customerBehind` fell through to `calls`, looked a
   * `mbos_travel_legs` id up among the calls, found nothing, and refused the
   * read. To the salesman who took it and to the manager approving the claim
   * it belongs to. It fails SHUT, which is the safe direction and exactly why
   * it survived: the only screen that shows one is the claim review, and a
   * broken image there reads as a photograph nobody took.
   *
   * It cannot be answered by the customer's scope either, though a leg often
   * names a shop. An odometer photograph is not evidence about the customer —
   * it is evidence about the SALESMAN, on a record somebody is eventually paid
   * out on. Read through the shop, a telecaller holding that book could open a
   * colleague's expense evidence.
   */
  if (row.parentType === "mbos_travel_leg") {
    return canReadTravelLegPhoto(row.parentId);
  }

  if (row.parentType === "mbos_expense") {
    return canReadExpenseAttachment(row.parentId);
  }

  /*
   * A VISIT'S PHOTOGRAPHS AND VOICE NOTE, A SAMPLE'S PROOF, A TASK'S PHOTO —
   * and every one of them was a 404, to everybody.
   *
   * The same fall-through the attendance selfie and the odometer photograph
   * were rescued from, three parent types over: `customerBehind` looked an
   * `mbos_visits` id up among `calls`, found nothing, and refused. The handset
   * has uploaded a shop photo, a customer photo and a voice note on visits
   * since it shipped, and no manager could ever open one — which is why the
   * Visits screen could only print how many there were.
   *
   * Read as field evidence: the salesman who took it, and whoever holds a
   * Sales Dashboard screen that shows it with him in scope. Then, failing
   * that, the customer's own scope for a visit or a sample — a shop photo is
   * also a fact about the shop, and a CRM user who may open the account may
   * see what it looks like. A task names no customer, so it stops at the first.
   */
  if (row.parentType === "mbos_visit") {
    const [visit] = await db
      .select({ salesmanId: mbosVisits.salesmanId, customerId: mbosVisits.customerId })
      .from(mbosVisits)
      .where(eq(mbosVisits.id, row.parentId));
    if (!visit) return false;
    if (await canReadSalesmansOwnEvidence(visit.salesmanId, ["sales.journeys", "sales.people"])) {
      return true;
    }
    return customerInScope(visit.customerId);
  }
  if (row.parentType === "mbos_sample") {
    const [sample] = await db
      .select({ salesmanId: mbosSamples.salesmanId, customerId: mbosSamples.customerId })
      .from(mbosSamples)
      .where(eq(mbosSamples.id, row.parentId));
    if (!sample) return false;
    if (await canReadSalesmansOwnEvidence(sample.salesmanId, ["sales.samples", "sales.leads"])) {
      return true;
    }
    return customerInScope(sample.customerId);
  }
  if (row.parentType === "mbos_task") {
    const [task] = await db
      .select({ userId: mbosTasks.assignedToUserId })
      .from(mbosTasks)
      .where(eq(mbosTasks.id, row.parentId));
    if (!task) return false;
    return canReadSalesmansOwnEvidence(task.userId, ["sales.tasks"]);
  }

  const customerId = await customerBehind(row.parentType, row.parentId);
  if (!customerId) return false;

  // Drizzle, not raw SQL, and no cast. This was a hand-written query handing
  // snake_case columns to a function that reads camelCase ones, with `as never`
  // silencing the compiler: `kind` was absent and `ownerId` was undefined, so
  // assignedUserId() answered null and EVERY read was refused. It failed shut,
  // which is the safe direction and the reason nobody noticed — no screen had
  // ever displayed an attachment to notice with.
  const [customer] = await db
    .select({
      kind: customers.kind,
      ownerId: customers.ownerId,
      salesAmId: customers.salesAmId,
    })
    .from(customers)
    .where(eq(customers.id, customerId));
  if (!customer) return false;

  try {
    await assertCustomerInScope(customer);
    return true;
  } catch {
    /* A FIELD COLLECTION OR A FIELD COMPLAINT IS ALSO THE SALESMAN'S EVIDENCE.
       The customer's scope answers for the CRM; a sales manager is scoped by
       the salesman, not the book, and the Payments and Field reports screens
       show these photographs to exactly that person. Asked only after the
       customer's scope has said no, so it can widen and never narrow. */
    if (row.parentType === "payment_receipt") {
      const [receipt] = await db
        .select({ by: paymentReceipts.reportedById })
        .from(paymentReceipts)
        .where(eq(paymentReceipts.id, row.parentId));
      if (receipt?.by && (await canReadSalesmansOwnEvidence(receipt.by, ["sales.payments"]))) {
        return true;
      }
    }
    if (
      row.parentType === "mbos_lead" &&
      row.uploadedById &&
      (await canReadSalesmansOwnEvidence(row.uploadedById, ["sales.leads"]))
    ) {
      return true;
    }
    if (row.parentType === "complaint") {
      const [complaint] = await db
        .select({ by: complaints.loggedByUserId })
        .from(complaints)
        .where(eq(complaints.id, row.parentId));
      if (complaint?.by && (await canReadSalesmansOwnEvidence(complaint.by, ["sales.field-reports"]))) {
        return true;
      }
    }
    /* A complaint is also the ERP's "customer request". Whoever may open the
       ERP's complaints screen decides complaints and may open their
       photographs and credit notes, whether or not that customer is in a CRM
       book of theirs — the rule the request's files were read under before
       they became the complaint's (0184). */
    if (row.parentType === "complaint") {
      const ctx = await resolveScope();
      const { canReadErpAttachment } = await import("@/lib/erp/attachments");
      return canReadErpAttachment(ctx.user.id, "complaint", row.parentId);
    }
    return false;
  }
}

export async function GET(
  _request: Request,
  { params }: { params: Promise<{ id: string }> },
) {
  const { id } = await params;

  const user = await getCurrentUser();
  if (!user) return new NextResponse("Not signed in", { status: 401 });

  // A file somebody may not see and a file that does not exist answer the
  // same way — otherwise this endpoint reports which customers exist.
  if (!(await canRead(id))) {
    return new NextResponse("Not found", { status: 404 });
  }

  const [row] = await db
    .select()
    .from(attachments)
    .where(eq(attachments.id, id));
  if (!row) return new NextResponse("Not found", { status: 404 });

  /* A file whose bytes retention has already taken. Without this the read
     reaches storage, finds nothing and answers 502 — which reads as a broken
     backend and sends somebody looking for a fault that is not there. The row
     is deliberately kept (see `sweepAttendanceSelfies`), so "it existed and is
     gone" is a thing this endpoint can actually say. */
  if (row.status === "removed") {
    return new NextResponse("This file has been deleted", { status: 410 });
  }

  try {
    const bytes = await fileStorage.read(row.storedRef);
    return new NextResponse(bytes, {
      headers: {
        "Content-Type": row.contentType,
        "Content-Length": String(row.sizeBytes),
        // inline: a telecaller wants to look at the photograph, not download it.
        "Content-Disposition": `inline; filename="${encodeURIComponent(row.filename)}"`,
        // Private and short-lived: the URL carries no proof of anything, so a
        // shared cache holding it would be handing the file to whoever asks.
        "Cache-Control": "private, max-age=300, no-store",
      },
    });
  } catch {
    return new NextResponse("Attachment could not be read", { status: 502 });
  }
}

export async function removeAttachment(attachmentId: string): Promise<Result> {
  const ctx = await resolveScope();
  const [row] = await db
    .select()
    .from(attachments)
    .where(eq(attachments.id, attachmentId));
  if (!row) return err("That attachment no longer exists.", "not_found");

  await db
    .update(attachments)
    .set({
      status: "removed",
      parentType: null,
      parentId: null,
      removedAt: new Date(),
      updatedAt: new Date(),
      updatedById: ctx.user.id,
    } as never)
    .where(eq(attachments.id, attachmentId));

  return okVoid(`${row.filename} removed`);
}

export async function sweepOrphans(): Promise<{ swept: number }> {
  const config = await getConfig();
  const cutoff = new Date(
    Date.now() - config["attachments.orphanCleanupHours"] * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  );

  const orphans = await db
    .select()
    .from(attachments)
    .where(and(isNull(attachments.parentId), lt(attachments.uploadedAt, cutoff)));

  for (const row of orphans) {
    // The bytes go here: nothing ever pointed at them, so there is no
    // interaction record being destroyed.
    if (row.storedRef) await fileStorage.remove(row.storedRef).catch(() => {});
    await db
      .update(attachments)
      .set({ status: "removed", removedAt: new Date(), updatedAt: new Date() })
      .where(eq(attachments.id, row.id));
  }

  return { swept: orphans.length };
}

export async function sweepAttendanceSelfies(): Promise<{ swept: number }> {
  const config = await getConfig();
  const cutoff = new Date(
    Date.now() - config["mbos.attendance.selfieRetentionHours"] * 60 * 60 * 1000,
  );

  const expired = await db
    .select({ id: attachments.id, storedRef: attachments.storedRef })
    .from(attachments)
    .where(
      and(
        eq(attachments.parentType, "mbos_attendance"),
        eq(attachments.status, "available"),
        lt(attachments.uploadedAt, cutoff),
      ),
    );

  for (const row of expired) {
    /* The bytes first, the row second. The other order leaves a row saying
       "removed" over a file still sitting in storage, which is the one state
       nothing later would ever go back and tidy. */
    if (row.storedRef) await fileStorage.remove(row.storedRef).catch(() => {});
    await db
      .update(attachments)
      .set({ status: "removed", removedAt: new Date(), updatedAt: new Date() })
      .where(eq(attachments.id, row.id));
  }

  return { swept: expired.length };
}

The paging test uses seven bills a day so a broken cursor cannot pass on a page boundary. Cast a stored date with the zone. bill date::timestamp at time zone 'Asia/Kolkata' , never ::timestamptz . Exclude unstated from every money total. If a new figure is "what is owed", filter payment position = 'stated' like recomputeOutstanding does.

Sales Bills is the ledger: every bill raised to customers in your book , one financial year at a time, with what was billed, what has been paid against it, what is left and how late it is. Open a bill number to see what was ordered on it. If you want who owes us , one line per customer, use Outstanding. Sales Bills answers what did we bill .

search.heading: The screen at a glance
search.text: Sales Bills for the current financial year. Sales bills Export Bills. 1,240 Outstanding. ₹14,20,000 Overdue bills. 96 Oldest band. ₹2,10,000 Collected. ₹1,02,00,000 Aging of outstanding balance.

search.heading: Reading a bill
search.text: Column Means Bill no The bill's number — usually the Tally number, like MMI/26-27/1119 Date The bill date Due The bill's own due date, or the bill date plus the customer's credit period Amount What was billed Paid What accounts have confirmed against it Balance Amount minus paid Overdue Days past the due date, while there is a balance Bucket Which aging band the balance sits in Status Unpaid, Partly paid or Paid Paid means confirmed. A payment the customer says they made, or one that is still waiting for accounts, is not in the Paid column. A bill stays at its full balance until accounts confirm the money.

search.heading: Financial years
search.text: The ledger shows one financial year at a time — April to March — and opens on the current one. Bill numbers carry the year too: MMI/ 26-27 /1119 is a bill from April 2026 to March 2027. Pick an earlier year from the year filter; the list of years goes back to the first bill on record. The figures across the top and the aging strip always describe the whole year you picked , whatever page you are on.

search.heading: Looking at one customer's bills
search.text: From a customer's record, See all bills opens this screen filtered to that customer. The title names them; clear it to go back to everybody.

search.heading: Recording a payment against a bill
search.text: Open the row menu and choose Record a payment. Only offered while the bill has a balance. Fill in what came. Amount received (up to the balance), how it came, the reference, the date received — and for a cheque, the date written on it. Save. If you hold the accounts desk's right to confirm money, it is confirmed and the balance drops. Otherwise it is reported and waits for accounts; the balance stays until they confirm it.

search.heading: Questions people ask
search.text: Why is every bill from last year missing?. The ledger opens on the current financial year. Pick last year from the year filter. To see everything still owed regardless of year, use Outstanding. A bill number has the order number added on the end.. When two orders share a Tally number, the second is numbered with its order number added — MMI/26-27/1119/4521 — so every bill number is unique. The customer paid but the bill still says Unpaid.. The money has not been confirmed by accounts yet. Why can I not export?. Exporting the ledger is a manager action in the CRM. What is on a bill?. Click the bill number. A sales bill is the order — the lines are the order's lines.

Sales Bills is the ledger of what Mahek billed. Bills arrive from the order sheet (a sales bill is the order), from accounts entering them, and from Tally's receivables report. What a bill is worth is the sheet's; what has been paid against it is only ever the app's, rebuilt from confirmed receipts. This tab explains where bills come from, how they are numbered, how paid and owed are decided, and how the ledger is cut and paged.

search.heading: A sales bill is the order
search.text: One bill per order, valued as the sum of its lines. Bills are projected from the order sheet's Order Details tab, one per order. The amount is the sum of every line's final amount — final amount is per line, and about half of orders have more than one line. The bill date is the dispatch date, or the order date where there is none. Opening a bill number shows the order's lines. The Order Details tab carries a Tally bill number on almost every line and the amount on all of them; that ledger is what Sales Bills is meant to show. Sourcing bills from the Payment Status tab alone left the screen empty whenever that tab had not been pulled — bills missing because of a second document rather than because there were none.

search.heading: Numbering
search.text: A bill number must be unique across the whole table, not just within one import. How a sheet order gets its bill number. The import used to decide numbering by counting Tally numbers inside its own batch, blind to a bill somebody typed in, one the Payment Status path wrote, or one a half-finished run left behind. The insert threw after thousands of rows had already landed. Reading existing numbers first means one unusable number cannot cost the other ten thousand rows.

search.heading: Paid, owed, and the payment position
search.text: The sheet never writes money. No receipt, no paid amount, no status, no outstanding — not in any column, not by any path. Whether money arrived is the app's to record and nobody else's. Field Who writes it How Amount The sheet (or accounts entering a bill) As billed Paid amount The app only Rebuilt from confirmed receipts every time, never incremented Status The app only Unpaid, partly paid or paid, from paid against amount Payment position The sheet on insert only ; afterwards the app stated (owed) or unstated Where nobody has said, a bill past its due date is owed. A bill the order sheet creates lands stated : its whole amount is open and it ages from its due date like any other bill. The one exception is the sheet's Payment Status tab saying Received — that bill lands unstated , held out of outstanding, aging, collections, the slow-payer flag and reminders, because the office has written down that the money came. Confirming it is still accounts' job. A person, not a sheet, settles a bill. Recording or confirming a receipt against a bill marks it stated and records when somebody decided. A later sheet pass never moves it back — the position is written on insert and never on update.

search.heading: The due date
search.text: The bill's own due date, or the bill date plus the credit period in force: the term agreed on the order, then the customer's standing term, then days.

search.heading: Cut by financial year
search.text: One financial year at a time, current by default. Ten thousand bills across three years is not a list anybody scrolls, and Mahek's own bill numbers already carry the year. The ledger is filtered to one April-to-March year on the server; the year list runs from the first bill on record to today. The totals describe the year, the table is a page. Paging is over what is filtered in. The figures across the top, the aging strip and the export all describe the whole filtered year ; only the table is cut into pages. A page that changed the totals under it would show a different figure on every click. A paged read needs a tie-breaker. Thousands of bills share a bill date. Every sort ends with the bill's id, so a bill never appears on two pages and another on none.

search.heading: Aging
search.text: The open balance is banded by days past the due date, using as the lower bounds. The same bands are used on Outstanding and in collections, and they are meant to line up with the follow-up stages so two screens never disagree about how late an account is. Clicking a band filters the table to exactly the bills the band counted.

search.heading: Recording money from the ledger
search.text: The row's Record a payment writes a receipt against that bill. Somebody holding payment.confirm is confirmed as they write it; everybody else reports, and the bill does not move until accounts confirm. The form offers the bill's whole unconfirmed balance — money merely reported against it is never subtracted from what can be recorded.

search.heading: Who sees which bills
search.text: A telecaller sees bills of customers in their own book; a manager on team scope sees their team's. Export is drawn for CRM managers.

search.heading: Every setting that shapes the ledger
Where the code and the intent disagree today
search.text: The ledger does not say which bills are not stated. The top Outstanding figure, the Overdue bills count and each row's balance include unstated bills as if they were owed, and nothing on the ledger marks them. Outstanding and Payment Follow-up leave them out, so the ledger's open total is higher than the same book's outstanding. - The ledger's "Collected" is paid amount on the year's bills , which is confirmed money — correct — but it is money against bills raised that year, not money received that year. - Export is decided by "manager in the CRM", not by the right to export customers , and the export address belongs to the Accounts app. - Bills, Outstanding and Payment Follow-up describe "not stated" in old words. Since October 2026 an unstated sheet bill means the Payment Status tab says received , not nobody has spoken .

The Call Log is a pure engine ( buildQueue ) fed by one service ( queue-service.ts ) and settled once a day into queue snapshots . The screen renders what the service returns; saving a call goes through saveInteraction , which ends by computing and storing the next-step sentence on the call. Every code block below is cut from the source this deployment was built from.

search.heading: A request, end to end
search.text: GET /crm/call-log.

search.heading: buildQueue
search.text: The whole pipeline: reasons → unreachable short-circuit → four windows → whole-customer suppression → rank → cap.

search.heading: The reasons and their weights
search.text: A stored queue.tierWeights replaces the default object wholesale, so weightOf falls back per kind — a blob written before a kind existed would otherwise give it undefined , and undefined arithmetic does not throw, it silently poisons the sort.

search.heading: Ordering
search.text: typicalOrderPaise is a cache on customers.typical order paise , written by writeCycle in lib/recompute.ts from approved orders over queue.orderValueLookbackDays . Fix a wrong value by re-running the recompute, never by updating the row.

search.heading: The stock-check day
search.text: routineDayFor is also read by the lead-nurture engine for the repeat-order call — change it and both move.

search.heading: Windows and suppression
search.text: The four windows strip reason kinds ; suppressionReason holds the whole customer . It is read before the "emptied by a window" sentence on purpose: a do-not-contact customer whose only reason was an order ask must be explained as do-not-contact, not as a cooldown. The predicates that decide what each window strips:

search.heading: The no-answer ladder
search.text: The count is consecutiveNoAnswerSql in queue-service.ts : outbound no answer calls since the latest call with any other non-null outcome.

search.heading: Saving a call
search.text: saveInteraction ( lib/services/interaction-service.ts ) validates outside the transaction, then writes everything in one transaction : the order ( pending approval ), reminders from the outcome and next actions, the complaint, the calls row, opportunities, timeline events, product lines, and the customer's last call date / last contact date / last order date / do not contact . Recomputes (buying cycle, inactivity, outstanding, follow-up state) run after commit. An idempotency key that already exists returns the stored next step and Already logged — a double-click cannot show a second answer.

search.heading: The next step is stored, not cached
search.text: Never let a recompute touch these. lib/recompute.ts must not learn to rebuild the next step columns. A cache answers "when is the next call" and is rebuilt when the answer changes; these answer "what did we tell the person who logged this call, on that day", and rebuilding them destroys the question. Same kind of mark as orders.approved at .

search.text: - Module: , enforced by the layout through requireModule . - No capability is checked on the read path; the write path relies on resolveScope() + assertCustomerInScope() and the discount level for order lines. - Scope is scopeForUser → user ids → scopedToUsers(ids) . Whose book is ASSIGNED TO SQL :

search.heading: Configuration the engine reads
search.text: Every key is in lib/config/registry.ts and stored in app settings ; reads go through getConfig() (30-second cache). The How it works tab shows each one's live value.

search.heading: Changing the Call Log safely
search.text: Put the rule in the engine, and only there. A new reason, window or suppression belongs in engines/queue.ts . next-step.ts re-asks buildQueue , so the "comes back on" sentence follows automatically — never re-derive a rule in a second place. Make every threshold a setting. Add the key to registry.ts (with a Config type entry), read it through QueueConfig . No number a manager might change is a constant. Suppress, never drop. Anything that keeps a customer off the list must return a sentence for the held-back strip. Give a new reason kind everything it needs. A weight in DEFAULT TIER WEIGHTS , a tone in REASON TONE (queue-screen), a short name in REASON BADGE (call panel), wording in describe() (next-step), and a filter pill if it is one. Test it in engines.test.ts first. The engine is pure; a rule without a test is a rule nobody can tell has broken.

The Call Log is your day's work. Every morning it lists the customers you should ring, in the order you should ring them , and every name carries the reason it is there. You work it top to bottom: call, log what happened, move to the next row. The numbers on this page — how many days, how many attempts — are the settings your CRM is using right now, read live. If a manager changes one on the Settings screen, this page changes with it.

search.heading: The screen at a glance
search.text: The Call Log, for a telecaller working their own book. Call Log Re-prioritise Call Customer A 12 of 48 worked 25% Connected today. 9 Connect rate. 75% Missed. 3 Orders today. 4 Booked today. ₹1.8L To work 36 Reminder due 4 No answer 6 Due to reorder 17 Check-in due 5 Leads 3 Inactive 2 j / k to move · Enter to open the call panel 7 customers held back today — nothing disappears silently

search.heading: Your day, step by step
search.text: Open the Call Log. The list is put together the first time anybody opens it each morning and then stays settled for the day — the order does not reshuffle under you while you work. The only thing that can jump in during the day is a reminder falling due: a callback you promised is added at the top. Start at the top row. The first row is your next call. Press Call (or Enter ) to open the call panel. The panel shows who they are, what they buy, what they owe, their last three calls — and the reason you are ringing. Make the call, then log what happened. Choose how the interaction happened, then the outcome, then fill in what the outcome asks for. Details are in Logging a call below. Read what happens next, then move on. After saving, a small window tells you when this customer comes back to your Call Log and why . Press Next customer — or use Save & next ▸ in the panel to save and move in one go. When the list is empty. You will see Queue cleared for today . The suggested next work is the Payment Follow-up list.

search.heading: Reading a row: what each reason means
search.text: Every customer is on the list for at least one reason. The colour tells you how urgent it is: red is overdue, amber is due today or needs attention, purple is routine sales work, grey is lower priority. Reason on the row Short name in the panel What it means What to do Payment overdue N days – ₹X Payment overdue Collections wants a call now. Only shown when payments are switched on for the Call Log (currently ). Chase the payment. Reminder N days overdue – note Reminder overdue A callback somebody promised is late. Ring them — they are expecting it. Reminder due today – note Reminder due today A promised callback is today. Ring them today. Order overdue by N full cycles Order overdue They have missed at least one whole order cycle. Ask for the order. Order overdue by N days / Order due today Order due Their order is due by their own buying pattern. Ask for the order. Stock check – orders every N days Stock check They are partway through their cycle. A good time to ask what is left on the shelf. Ask about stock, take the order if there is one. Never ordered – N days since last contact Never ordered A lead that has not bought yet. Try for a first order. No contact for N days – cycle not established yet Check-in overdue A customer whose buying pattern is not known yet, and it has been a while. Check in. Gone quiet – N cycles since their last order Stopped ordering They used to buy and have stopped. Ranked below orders that are merely due, on purpose. Ask why they stopped. Check-in due – N days since last contact Check-in due Routine check-in for a customer whose pattern is not known yet. Check in. Unreachable – N attempts, no answer Cannot reach them Rung several times in a row with no answer. Decide what happens next — a different number, a visit, or leave them. No answer – attempt N No answer – try again A retry after an earlier unanswered call. Ring again. Order in progress – status Order in progress An order is waiting for accounts or dispatch. Check on their order if they ask. The row also shows the contact person, phone, last order date, how long since anybody spoke to them, and the last note anybody wrote. Read the last note before you dial.

search.heading: Logging a call
search.text: The call panel, logging an outbound call that ended in an order. Customer A · contact person · phone. Reminder overdue Stock check We Called Them They Called Us Order Received Order Taken No Order No Answer Payment Promised Follow-up … 2 products · 14 cans · 152 L Confirm dispatch Send price list Save log Save & next ▸

search.heading: What each outcome asks you for
search.text: Outcome You must fill in What it does Order Taken Products and quantities Creates an order waiting for accounts to approve. No Order Why there was no order (one choice) They will not be asked for an order again for a few days — see Why is somebody missing below. No Answer Why (no response, busy, switched off…) Starts the retry ladder. The panel tells you which attempt this is. Payment Promised — Creates a payment-promise reminder, days out unless you set another date. Follow-up What you are waiting for Creates a reminder, day out unless you set another date. Complaint What they are asking for, category, description; photographs optional Raises a complaint (or adds to an open one of the same kind). Not Interested Why; whether there is a "later"; a date if there is "They asked us not to call again" marks the customer do not contact . Casual Talk Purpose Records the contact. Transport Follow-up — Records a delivery chase. For a call they made, you also choose who called (owner, purchase, accounts…) and why — answer those before the outcome. A common mistake. Logging an order that came in on WhatsApp as We Called Them → Order Taken . Use Order Received instead and give the order date — otherwise the record says you rang them on a day you did not.

search.heading: After you save: when they come back
search.text: The window that opens after a save tells you, in one fixed sentence, when this customer comes back to your Call Log : Comes back to your Call Log on Mon 1 Sep — 13 days away Ask for the order — they are due to reorder. The badge beside it tells you what kind of date that is: Promised. A callback the customer asked for. You owe them this call on that day. Scheduled. The date the rules give today. It moves if they order, pay or ask for a callback before then. Needs a decision. Nobody can reach them. There is no next call until somebody decides what to do. Nothing scheduled. Marked do not contact, or nothing brings them back within four months. If you have just promised a callback, the window offers Hold other calls until date . Press it to stop the Call Log asking you about orders or check-ins for this customer until the day you promised — money and reminders are never held.

search.heading: Customers held back today
search.text: The held-back strip, opened. 7 customers held back today. Nobody disappears from the Call Log without a reason. If you expected somebody and they are not there, open the held-back strip — the sentence beside their name is the rule that kept them off today. The How it works tab explains each rule.

search.heading: When nobody answers
search.text: You do not need to remember when to try again. The Call Log brings them back: The no-answer ladder. Any answered call puts them back to normal.. The same-day wait is hour(s). After unanswered calls in a row the customer is marked Unreachable and the row asks you to decide what happens next instead of ringing again.

search.heading: Skipping and closing an account
search.text: From the row menu (⋯): - Skip for today — takes them off today's list. You must say why; the reason is recorded and shown in the held-back strip. They come back tomorrow if they are still due. - Request deactivation — asks a manager to close the account (shop shut, duplicate, not a customer). The manager decides on the Close / Reopen screen. Until then the row says Deactivation already requested . - Send WhatsApp instead and See their bills open those screens for this customer.

search.heading: Keyboard shortcuts
search.text: Key Does j Move down the list k Move up the list Enter Open the call panel on the selected row Inside the panel, ◀ Previous and Next ▶ walk the list in the order it is shown.

search.heading: For managers: the team view
search.text: A manager sees the whole team's Call Log by default, with an extra Assigned to column saying whose call each row is (or Unassigned , which is the one to look at first). Switch to My book in the header to see only your own. A telecaller always sees only their own book.

search.heading: Why is somebody (not) on my list?
search.text: A customer I expected is not on the list and not in the held-back strip either.. They have no reason to be called today: not yet at their stock-check day, a lead contacted within the last days, or nothing due. Nothing is wrong — their day has not come. It says 'Already called today'.. Somebody — you or a colleague — logged a call with them today. Even a due reminder does not bring them back the same day. They ordered four days ago. Why no stock check?. After an order there is a quiet period of up to days (shorter for customers who order more often than that). Somebody who just ordered is serving themselves. A reminder you set still comes through. I told them 'no order' two days ago and they are not on the list.. A No Order answer buys a few days before the Call Log asks them for an order again. Only the order question is held — a reminder, a payment or a check-in still shows. It says 'WhatsApp sent … cooldown left'.. A WhatsApp message to them was confirmed sent in the last days. A message you copied but did not confirm does not count. A due reminder overrides this. It says 'Active in the order system'.. They have an order still open on the order sheet's Taken Order tab. Calling them for another order would be asking twice. It says 'On the sales team's lead funnel'.. The field sales team is working this lead towards an order, so the Call Log does not ask for one as well. Somebody owes a lot of money but is not on my Call Log.. Payment chasing lives on the Payment Follow-up screen. It only appears on the Call Log when a manager switches that on (currently ). The list is shorter than I expected.. The Call Log shows at most customers a day. The progress count includes everyone who qualified. It says 'Dealt with since the list was settled'.. They were on this morning's list but no longer need a call — for example they ordered, or somebody already rang them.

The Call Log answers one question every morning: of everybody in this book, who should be rung today, and in what order? It is not a contact schedule. It chases orders — each customer is called from their own buying pattern, and everything else (reminders, leads, check-ins, money) is fitted around that. This tab explains every rule that decides the list, why it is that rule, and the setting that changes it. Every value quoted is the one your CRM is using right now; amber means a manager has changed it from the shipped default.

search.heading: How a customer gets onto the list
search.text: From the whole book to today's list. Three things are deliberate about this shape: 1. Nobody vanishes silently. A customer the rules keep off the list goes into the held-back strip with a sentence saying why. A telecaller must always be able to find out why somebody they expected is missing. 2. Windows silence a kind of call, not the customer. A customer who ordered yesterday still appears if a reminder or a check-in is due — only the order chasing is removed. 3. The list is settled once a day. It is built on the first read of the morning and then kept, so the order does not reshuffle under somebody halfway down it.

search.heading: The reasons, and how they are ranked
search.text: Every customer on the list has at least one reason . The strongest reason decides where they sit. The ranking is a configurable weight per reason: Money and promises first, then orders that should already have happened, then routine work. A callback the customer asked for is a promise; not making it is worse than any order missed. "Stopped ordering" deliberately sits below every order that is merely due: the "why did you stop" conversation is worth having, but at one time there were more lapsed customers than active ones, and ranked higher they pushed the people about to reorder off the bottom of the list.

search.heading: Within the same reason: what the call is worth
search.text: Two customers both "due to order" are not equal. Within a reason, the list is ordered by what the call is worth : - A payment call is worth the amount owed. - An order call is worth the customer's typical order — the median of their own approved orders over the last days. Never a figure from the catalogue: the product master has no prices. - A prediction (order due, stock check, overdue, stopped) is discounted by how sure we are of the customer's pattern . Somebody who orders every 29, 30, 31 days is a safer bet than somebody who orders after 15, 45, 22 and 60. A customer whose confidence has never been measured is not discounted. Missing information must never demote anybody. After value, ties are broken by: outstanding balance, gap to target, longest since anybody spoke to them.

search.heading: Calling from the customer's own buying cycle
search.text: Every customer with enough history has a buying cycle — the typical number of days between their orders — and a confidence in it. The Call Log uses the cycle to decide every order-related reason. The stock check: before the order is due. For a customer with a measured cycle, the Call Log rings partway through the cycle to ask what is left on the shelf. The day is % of the cycle, moved by up to points by confidence: a very regular customer is called later , closer to the day they really order; an erratic one earlier , because the honest answer to a guess is a wider net. Customers whose cycle is days or shorter get no stock check — somebody buying every week already knows their shelf. Their order is chased on its due date like everyone else's. A 30-day customer Confidence unknown or 50% Very regular (100%) Erratic (0%) Stock check from day 21 24 18 Worked with the shipped settings (70%, swing 10). Due, overdue, and stopped. - Order due — the day their cycle says they should order, and until they have missed a whole cycle. - Order overdue by a full cycle — at least one whole cycle missed. - Stopped ordering — they have gone × their own cycle without an order. The same multiple marks the customer Inactive on their record, so the Call Log and the customer list cannot disagree about who has lapsed. One customer with a 30-day cycle, across one cycle, with the shipped settings: Days since their last order What the Call Log does 1 – 15 Quiet no order chased — they have just bought 16 – 20 Nothing — no reason to ring yet 21 – 29 Stock check ask what is left on the shelf 30 Order due today 31 – 59 Order overdue 60 onwards Stopped ordering ask why they stopped Customers without a measured cycle. A customer needs enough orders before a cycle means anything. Until then they get a steady check-in : due after days without contact, overdue at one and a half times that. A guessed cycle never earns a stock-check or due date — chasing on a guess rings a quarterly buyer every month. Leads. A lead who has never ordered is called every days, counted from the last contact (or from when they were added, if nobody has spoken to them yet). Two kinds of lead are not prospected: a shop we deliver to through a distributor (a third-party customer ), and a lead the field team is working on the lead funnel.

search.heading: What holds a customer back
search.text: Some rules remove one kind of call and leave the rest. Others hold the whole customer back for the day.

search.heading: Windows: silence the order question, not the customer
search.text: Quiet after an order. No order is chased within days of the last one — or the customer's own cycle, if that is shorter and measured . Somebody who ordered days ago is serving themselves. The cap matters: a flat 15 days used to run past the due date of anybody ordering every week, so the customers ordering most often were chased last, and late. Now every customer follows one rule: quiet until their order is due, chased from the day it is. What the customer said last time. After an answered call, the order question rests for a time that depends on the answer: Without this, a customer past their call day returns to the top of the list every day until they order — which punishes the telecaller for working it. Only the ask is silenced; a reminder, a debt or a check-in still comes through. Held by a promised callback. When a telecaller promises a callback and presses Hold other calls until… , order and check-in calls for that customer stop until the promised day. Money, reminders and "unreachable" are never held. On the lead funnel. A lead the sales team is climbing the lead ladder with is not cold-called by the office and not chased for a reorder — otherwise two people chase one customer, neither knowing about the other. The lead still appears in the held-back strip with the reason.

search.heading: Held back for the whole day
search.text: These are checked in this order, and the first one that applies is the sentence shown: Order Held back because A due reminder overrides it? 1 Marked do not contact No — a standing instruction 2 Skipped today , with the reason given No 3 Already called today by anybody (setting: ) No — the contact has happened 4 Active in the order system — an open line on the Taken Order tab (setting: ) No — they have already ordered 5 Waiting before the next no-answer retry No 6 WhatsApp confirmed sent within days Yes Why a reminder beats the WhatsApp cooldown. The cooldown used to be the one rule that did not bend. A marketing message sent on Tuesday silently cancelled a call promised for Wednesday — a broken promise caused by something we chose to do. A reminder now overrides the quiet window, the "told us no" window and the WhatsApp cooldown. It does not override do-not-contact, a call already made today, or an open order: the first is an instruction and the others mean the contact has already happened. Copied is not sent. Only a WhatsApp message a person confirmed as sent starts the cooldown. A message copied and never confirmed is a customer who may or may not have heard from us, and it is shown as exactly that.

search.heading: When nobody answers
search.text: The no-answer ladder. - The second attempt comes after hour(s), the same day. - Later attempts wait days — one rung per attempt, the last rung repeating. - After unanswered calls in a row the customer becomes Unreachable : one row, one reason, and a question for a person rather than a sixth ring. - Any answered call resets the count.

search.heading: The list is settled once a day
search.text: The first time a telecaller's Call Log is read on a working day, the list is stored . Every later read that day keeps that order and those reasons. During the day: - A customer who no longer needs a call (they ordered, somebody rang them) leaves the list and appears in the held-back strip as Dealt with since the list was settled . - A reminder falling due is added at the top — a promise outranks a settled list. - The list never grows by any other route, so somebody halfway down it is never pushed back up by a reshuffle. The Call Log shows at most customers (0 means no limit). The progress count still counts everybody who qualified.

search.heading: What saving a call does
search.text: Saving a call is one transaction : the call, any order, reminder or complaint it produced, and the customer's rolled-up figures are written together or not at all. Half-saved calls are how telecaller data goes wrong. Saving a call. What the telecaller is told is kept, and never rewritten. The sentence shown after saving — Comes back to your Call Log on Mon 1 Sep — is stored on the call. It is a record of what the telecaller was told on that day, not a forecast that is kept up to date. If the customer orders the next morning, the customer's real next call changes; the old sentence does not, and the difference is the record of what changed. The Call History screen shows these stored answers. An order is the customer saying yes, not the business. An order taken on a call waits for accounts to approve it . "Did the customer order" is true at once, and stops the Call Log chasing them; "did we sell anything" is only true after approval, and is what targets, EOD value and the buying cycle count.

search.heading: Who sees whose list
search.text: - A telecaller sees only their own book. They cannot widen it. - A manager sees their team (their direct reports and themselves) by default, and can switch to their own book. An admin sees everyone. - Whose book a customer is in is one definition used by every list in the CRM: a lead belongs to its owner; a customer to its sales account manager. A team list says whose call each row is, and says Unassigned in words — a call nobody owns is the one a manager most needs to see.

search.heading: Every setting that shapes the Call Log
Where the code and the intent disagree today
search.text: These were found while writing this page. They are listed so nobody is surprised by them; each is a candidate for a fix. Settings on the screen that change nothing. Lead call percentage , lead minimum / maximum days and Quiet days after "no order" ( queue.leadPercent , queue.leadMinDays , queue.leadMaxDays , queue.noOrderCooldownDays ) are shown on the Settings screen but no longer read by the Call Log. The "no order" quiet now comes from How long each answer buys above. Hour the queue is snapshotted ( queue.snapshotHour ) only changes a sentence — the list is settled on the first read of the day, whatever the hour. - Unreachable customers skip the hold-back checks. A customer who has reached the no-answer limit is listed even if marked do-not-contact or already called today. - A pending no-answer retry hides a due reminder for the length of the wait. - Only calls we made start the "told us no" quiet. An inbound "No order" buys none. - The retry ladder counts calendar days , though the setting's description says working days. - Re-prioritise re-reads the settled list; it does not rebuild it. Only an administrator's rebuild does. - The morning warm-up job builds lists without payment calls, so on days it runs before anybody opens the Call Log, payment reasons are missing from the settled list even when payments are switched on.

A complaint is a row in complaints with an opening line in complaint status history , photographs in attachments , and an SLA deadline computed from configuration. One writer, createComplaint , is shared by the Complaints dialog and the ERP's "Raise a customer request"; three other paths — the call panel, the collections Dispute raised outcome and the handset — insert complaints themselves. Reads, status changes, priority and resolution live in worklist-services.ts ; the hourly job escalates deadlines that pass.

search.heading: Raising one from the dialog
search.text: logComplaint → createComplaint.

search.heading: Changing status, priority and resolving
search.text: - A status into or out of a finished state (resolved, closed, rejected) requires complaint.resolve . - Changing priority recomputes sla due at from the complaint's creation time and the new priority's hours. - Every change writes a complaint status history row.

search.heading: The deadline job
search.text: runHourly selects complaints with sla due at in the past, resolved at null and sla escalated at null, stamps sla escalated at , and notifies managers and admins. It runs once per complaint.

search.heading: Access
search.text: - Module: . - Scope: listComplaints is narrowed to the reader's book; status and priority changes run customerOfComplaintInScope . - Photographs are read through /api/attachments/[id] , which follows the parent complaint's customer scope.
