MahekOne is Mahek Marketing India's connected workspace: one sign-in, one database, many apps . The Telecaller CRM, the Sales Dashboard, Accounts, HRMS, the ERP and the rest are not separate systems that exchange files — they are screens over the same tables, so a customer, an order or a payment is one record that every app reads. The field salesman's phone app (MBOS) is the one exception to "screens on this site": it keeps its own copy of the salesman's book on the handset and syncs with the same database. This page is the map for the rest of the documentation. It says what the apps are, who works in each, how information gets in, and the handful of rules that every app follows. The developer tab explains how it is built.

search.heading: The big picture
search.text: Everything MahekOne talks to, and where it runs. Three things about this shape are deliberate: 1. Only Caddy faces the internet. The app and the database publish no public port. Postgres is reachable only from the droplet itself, so a leaked database password is not, on its own, a way in. 2. The database sits next to the app. Every query is a loopback on the same machine rather than a round trip to another continent. That is most of why the screens are fast, and why the whole thing costs a few dollars a month. 3. Google Sheets are read, never written. The team still types into its workbooks; MahekOne pulls what they typed on a schedule and publishes it into the database. Nothing MahekOne does can change a cell. MahekOne ran on Vercel with a Neon database until August 2026. Some comments and older notes still talk about "a database in GMT" — that was Neon. The rule it produced (never turn a stored time into a date without naming the zone) still holds; see The working day below.

search.heading: The apps
search.text: Every app is an entry in one registry. Granting somebody an app is a row in the database, not a change to the code. Fourteen ids exist today: App Who works in it What it is for Telecaller CRM Telecallers and their managers The daily Call Log, payment follow-up, reminders, customers, leads and the end-of-day report. Salesman App (mobile only) Field salesmen MBOS, the Android app. Granting it gives a phone sign-in and nothing in the browser — there is no web screen and there never will be. Sales Dashboard Sales managers and the office end of the field team The field team's day, the journeys they walk, live location, approvals, targets and expenses. Accounts The accounts desk Order approvals, money coming in, the bill ledger, credit notes, outstanding, the sheet import. Formerly called Orders; old /orders links still work. Attendance and People (retired) — Its work moved into HRMS. The id is kept so old grants still resolve, but nothing draws it. Reports (retired) — The owner's figures moved into the Founder Command Centre. Kept for the same reason. HRMS HR, and every employee for their own check-in and leave Check in and out, leave, payroll, tasks, performance and the employee master. Admin Console Platform administrators Who opens what, settings, credentials, sheets, jobs, handsets, the audit log. Founder Command Centre The owner and named delegates Every app's figures on one screen, and what needs the owner today. Website Enquiries Whoever works enquiries in Sales, Accounts or HR Enquiries from the website and elsewhere, from first contact to delivery. ERP The factory and the godowns Purchase, quality tests, stock, production, packing, orders, dispatch and transport. Website Whoever edits the public site Products, pages, gallery and careers content for the public website. Hire Recruiters, interviewers, HR Role blueprints, the hiring pipeline, interviews, offers and onboarding — ending in a working MahekOne account. Documentation Anybody given it These pages. A mobile-only app never becomes a browser tile. The Salesman App is a real, grantable app — the Access screen offers it and the phone refuses to sign in without it — but the launcher, the app switcher and the "straight into it" redirect all leave it out. A salesman who holds only the Salesman App and signs in on the web lands on the launcher, which tells him there is nothing for him there. A retired app

search.heading: Signing in, and where you land
search.text: There is one sign-in for all of MahekOne , at /login . You can sign in with your work number or your email (or the personal mobile number HR holds for you), and either a password or a one-time code sent to your phone over WhatsApp, with SMS when WhatsApp does not deliver. Where you land depends on what you can open: - One app (in the browser) — straight into it. A single option is not a choice. - Several — the launcher at /apps . - None — the launcher, which says so plainly instead of showing a blank screen. A forgotten password is reset by the person themselves, either with an emailed link or with a code to their phone. Resetting ends every session on the account. A sign-in is also recorded as a row per person per day. That is a sign-in log, not attendance — attendance is the check-in in HRMS and on the handset, with its own screens.

search.heading: Who can open what
search.text: Access is decided in three layers, each narrower than the last. From a person to what they can do on one screen.

search.heading: An app, then its screens
search.text: - An app is granted to a person , from Admin Console → Access. The employee must be active in HRMS. Granting from the console can create the MahekOne account in the same step; the account starts unusable and the person sets a password from a single-use link. - Inside an app, screens (modules) can be withheld. Anything with a place in the app's sidebar or header is a module. No module rows means every module — so granting an app opens all of it, and it narrows only once somebody unticks a screen. A few desks (the lead calling desk, for example) are marked "off by default" and are not included in a whole-app grant. - Revoking an app removes its module rows too , so re-granting it later does not quietly come back narrowed. - Disabling a sign-in is not revoking access. A disabled account keeps its apps — somebody away for a month comes back to the book they left — but cannot sign in, and every session it had is ended.

search.heading: A role is a level; the app is the job
search.text: There are three levels, and the same three in every app : associate , manager , admin . The level is held per app , on the grant. There used to be four roles — telecaller, manager, accounts, admin — which mixed two ideas: two levels of seniority and two job titles borrowed from two particular apps. A field salesman ended up stored as a "telecaller". Now the job comes from the app: an associate in the CRM is a telecaller; an associate in Accounts is the accounts clerk; an associate on the Salesman App is the field salesman. One level, three jobs, decided by the grant. - What you may do is the union. Holding a power under any of your grants is holding it. - What you may see is decided per app. A person who is a manager on the Sales Dashboard and an associate in the CRM sees their team on the Sales Dashboard and only their own book in the CRM. - The money decisions belong to the Accounts app. Approving orders, confirming payments, issuing credit notes and moving an account to another salesperson are Accounts powers. A CRM manager cannot approve an order — the person chasing a target must not sign off the orders that hit it. - Admin of an app is admin of that app. Only Admin on the Admin Console is a platform administrator. An admin of HRMS or the ERP holds that app's manager powers plus whatever that app gives its own administrators — not the whole company. - Two powers that should not meet are named, not refused. When one person's grants combine roles that normally stay apart (taking an order and approving it, for instance), the Access review page says so in words, and every action carries the grant that allowed it in the audit log.

search.heading: Scope: my book or my team
search.text: Every list in MahekOne is narrowed by scope : Level in the app What a list shows Associate Only their own book. Nothing they choose can widen it. Manager Their team — the people who report directly to them, and themselves — by default. They can switch to My book . Admin Everybody, with the same switch to narrow to their own book. Anybody in Accounts Every book. The approval queue is nobody's own book. Anybody in the Founder Command Centre The whole company; delegates are narrowed by which screens they hold, not by whose book. Whose book a customer is in is one definition used by every list: a lead belongs to its owner; a customer to its sales account manager , falling back to the owner only where nobody has set one. A team list says whose each row is, and says Unassigned in words.

search.heading: How information gets in
search.text: The five ways data reaches the database.

search.heading: People typing in the apps
search.text: Most writes are a person pressing Save on a screen. Each save is checked on the server — whether the person may do it, whether the record is in their scope — however the button was drawn. A save that produces several records (a call that also takes an order and sets a reminder) is one transaction : all of it lands, or none of it.

search.heading: The MBOS handset
search.text: The field salesman works offline first . Everything he records — a visit, an order, a payment, a check-in selfie, a photograph of a meter — is written to the phone's own database and queued. When there is signal, the phone sends the queue and pulls back what changed in the office: his customers, products, price lists, tasks, approvals, the configuration. A record is never lost because a market had no signal; it waits in the queue until it can go. The office decides what the phone may hold. A salesman's phone carries only his own book, narrowed to the territory he has been allocated. With no territory allocated, a salesman's phone holds no shops — and says so — rather than carrying the whole company's book.

search.heading: Google Sheets
search.text: The team's workbooks — the order sheet (Order Details, Payment Status, Taken Order, Sales Party), the employee sheet, and the older field app's shop master and activity log — are read by a Google service account with read-only access. Each run lands rows in staging tables first, then a separate step publishes them into customers, orders and bills. A run that changes nothing in the sheet writes nothing. The droplet's cron runs the cycle every half hour, a lighter pass every hour, and a full compare plus every recompute once a night. See Google Sheets sync and scheduled jobs. The sheet never writes money. No sync, by any path, records a payment, sets what was paid on a bill, or changes outstanding. Whether money arrived is for a person to record. A bill imported from the sheet with no payment recorded either way is held out of outstanding and collections until somebody speaks for it. The sheet wins every column except a decision somebody made. If accounts approved or declined an order, or somebody reassigned an account, the next sync keeps that decision and records the disagreement for review rather than overwriting it.

search.heading: WhatsApp
search.text: WhatsApp runs through Wati. Wati reports delivery and replies back to MahekOne; MahekOne sends templates only when the owner has switched sending on. A message a telecaller copies to send by hand counts as sent only when they confirm it .

search.heading: The public website
search.text: Enquiries submitted on the public website are forwarded by the website's own backend to MahekOne, which refuses any request that does not carry the shared secret.

search.heading: Rules every app follows
search.text: Nothing business-critical is a constant. Every threshold a manager might want to change — how many days before a customer counts as inactive, how far a salesman may be from a shop to check in, how long a payment promise buys — is a setting , changed from a screen and audited. See Configuration, settings and secrets. Derived values are caches, rebuilt — never hand-edited. Buying cycles, outstanding balances, follow-up stages, slow-payer flags, last-contact dates and salesman scores are all worked out from the records underneath . If one is wrong, the fix is to re-run the rebuild, never to type over the number. The nightly job rebuilds all of them; the important ones are also rebuilt the moment something they depend on changes. A stored figure that somebody can edit is a figure that can disagree with the orders and payments behind it, and nobody can tell which is right. A figure that is always rebuilt from the records cannot drift. Money is paise. Every amount is stored as a whole number of paise (₹1 = 100 paise) and only turned into rupees on the way to the screen. Rupees with decimals are never stored, so no amount is ever off by a rounding error. The same number comes from the same place. A figure on a dashboard and the same figure on its own screen are read by the same function. Two screens never compute "outstanding" or "orders this month" two different ways. Suppressed, never silently dropped. Where a rule keeps something off a list — a customer held back from the Call Log, a shop with no map pin — the screen says so and says why. An empty screen with no explanation reads as broken.

search.heading: The working day is Asia/Kolkata
search.text: Every "today", "this week" and "this month" is the business date in India , whatever machine is asking. The day changes at the hour set in (0 means midnight), the working week is , and the zone itself is . A server's clock and a database's clock can each be in any zone. A call logged at 1 am IST is 7:30 pm the previous day in GMT, and a report that turned a stored time into a date without naming the zone would have put it on the wrong day. So the zone is always named, and automated tests fail the build on any query or screen that forgets.

search.heading: Keeping it safe
search.text: - Backups : the database is dumped nightly and three times during the working day, encrypted, and copied to Cloudflare R2; a weekly drill restores the newest copy and compares it. See Backups and recovery. - Credentials for outside services are held separately from ordinary settings and are never shown on a screen beyond their last four characters. See Configuration, settings and secrets. - Every decision is audited — who did it, under which app and level, and when.

search.heading: Where the code and the intent disagree today
search.text: - Admin of an app is no longer admin everywhere , but some project notes still say "admin holds everything everywhere". The code ( can in src/lib/capability-matrix.ts ) gives an app admin that app's manager powers only; only Admin on the Admin Console is a platform administrator. The comment directly above can still describes the old behaviour. - The "manager configuration screen" in the CRM is gone. Older notes place settings in the CRM; /crm/settings now permanently redirects to the Admin Console, where every app's settings live (the Sales Dashboard keeps its own screen for the field app's settings). - The time zone is a setting, but the database queries do not read it. decides the business date in the app, while every day window in SQL uses a fixed Asia/Kolkata constant. Changing the setting would make the two disagree. - A manager's team is direct reports only. Somebody who reports to a person who reports to the manager is not in the manager's team view.

Backups are two shell scripts on the droplet — deploy/backup.sh and deploy/restore.sh — run by the deploy user's crontab, plus DigitalOcean's own daily droplet snapshot. backup.sh dumps every database in the Postgres container with pg dump , gzips, sanity-checks, encrypts with gpg to a public key, uploads with a throwaway rclone container to an R2 bucket, prunes by age, and pings a healthcheck. restore.sh fetches, decrypts (with a private key brought in for the purpose), empties the database and loads the dump. None of this is application code; the app has no role in it.

search.heading: Map of the pieces
search.text: Piece Where What it does backup.sh /opt/mahekone/backup.sh (from deploy/backup.sh ) Modes: default (nightly), --intraday , --verify , --install-cron restore.sh /opt/mahekone/restore.sh --list-r2 , --from-r2 , a local file, --key Local copies /opt/mahekone/backups/ mahekone .sql.gz , mahekone intraday.sql.gz , db- … Log /opt/mahekone/backups/backup.log One line per step, [timestamp] mode: … Offsite R2 bucket R2 BUCKET daily/ , intraday/ , monthly/ Encryption BACKUP GPG RECIPIENT FILE A public key file on the droplet; the private key is never there Alert BACKUP HEALTHCHECK URL healthchecks.io: /start , success, /fail Snapshot DigitalOcean droplet backups Whole machine, daily; the only copy of .env

search.heading: Environment it reads (from /opt/mahekone/.env)
search.text: Variable Required Without it R2 ACCESS KEY ID , R2 SECRET ACCESS KEY , R2 ENDPOINT , R2 BUCKET For offsite Logs "R2 not configured — this backup exists ONLY on the droplet" BACKUP GPG RECIPIENT FILE For encryption Logs "the R2 copy is NOT encrypted" and uploads plaintext BACKUP HEALTHCHECK URL For alerts No pings; nobody is told about a failure

search.heading: A nightly run
search.text: backup.sh (daily or intraday). Detail Behaviour Lock flock on /tmp/mahekone-backup.lock ; an overlapping run exits 0 quietly Size floor A dump under 1,000,000 bytes is refused as "too small to be the database" Integrity gzip -t on every file before it is kept Other databases Found at run time ( pg database minus postgres , mahekone , the verify scratch DB); one failing does not stop the others, but the run ends failed and names it Encrypted temp files .gpg is removed from the droplet after upload; the local plaintext .sql.gz stays for the local retention Monthly date -u +%d = 01 at 20:45 UTC — i.e. the run in the early hours of the 2nd, IST Exit Any failed step trips the EXIT trap, which pings /fail with REASON and deletes a half-written dump

search.heading: The verify run
search.text: backup.sh --verify (Sunday 22:30 UTC, Monday 04:00 IST): 1. Picks the newest mahekone .sql.gz on the droplet; fails if there is none or it is more than 36 hours old. 2. Drops and recreates the scratch database restore verify , restores the dump into it, and times it. 3. Compares count( ) for customers , orders , bills , payment receipts , calls , users , audit log , attachments against live; a restored count below 90% of a non-empty live count is SHORT and fails the run. 4. If R2 is configured, lists daily/ for anything newer than 36 hours; fails if empty. 5. Drops restore verify whatever happened.

search.heading: Installing the schedule
search.text: It replaces any existing backup.sh lines and leaves the rest of the crontab alone: UTC IST Line 45 20 02:15 daily backup.sh 45 2,8,14 08:15, 14:15, 20:15 backup.sh --intraday 30 22 0 04:00 Monday backup.sh --verify

search.heading: One-time setup
search.text: Make the key on your own machine. Store backup-private.asc and its passphrase in the password manager with a second person able to reach them. Copy only the public half to the droplet and set BACKUP GPG RECIPIENT FILE=/opt/mahekone/backup-public.asc in .env . Create the alert. A healthchecks.io check, period 6 hours, grace 1 hour, two email recipients; its ping URL as BACKUP HEALTHCHECK URL . Lock the bucket. R2 → the backup bucket → Settings → Bucket lock rules: daily/ 30 days, intraday/ 7 days, monthly/ 365 days. Add object lifecycle rules deleting at the same ages plus a day. Once locked, backup.sh 's own prune is silently refused until objects age out — expected. Prove it. bash backup.sh --intraday should end uploaded with a .gpg file in restore.sh --list-r2 ; bash backup.sh --verify should list eight tables ok ; the healthcheck should show both.

search.heading: Restoring
search.text: What restore.sh does: 1. With --from-r2 , copies the object into backups/ . 2. If it ends in .gpg , imports --key into a temporary keyring, prompts for the passphrase, decrypts beside it, and reminds you to delete the key from the box. 3. Prints the file, size and date and requires you to type replace . 4. docker compose stop app . 5. Drops the drizzle and public schemas and recreates public — so the result is exactly the dump, with no leftover tables. 6. Loads the dump with ON ERROR STOP=1 , then docker compose start app . Keep the private key off the droplet if you can. Better than scp -ing the key to /tmp and shred -u -ing it afterwards: fetch and gpg --decrypt on your own machine, then copy the plain .sql.gz to the droplet and restore that. The private key then never touches the server. Restore another database (they were dumped with --clean ):

search.heading: The restore drill
search.text: If drill is gone, the restore replaced the database and the backups work. If it is still there, nothing was restored — stop and find out why.

search.heading: What a backup does not hold
search.text: Not in the dump Where it is instead /opt/mahekone/.env DigitalOcean snapshot only — keep a copy in the password manager Attachment bytes in an R2 attachments bucket That bucket (see Storage) Caddy's certificates ( caddy data volume) Re-issued automatically on a new box The APK and mbos.json in /opt/mahekone/downloads Every APK is archived in R2 by the release workflow

search.heading: Changing it safely
search.text: Re-install the cron after editing backup.sh. --install-cron rewrites only its own lines. backup.sh is not shipped by any workflow — copy it to the droplet by hand. Keep the prune in line with the bucket lock. The script's KEEP REMOTE ages and the lock rules should match; a script age shorter than the lock just fails quietly, a longer one leaves objects the lifecycle rule removes first. Never let cleanup.sh delete dumps. deploy/cleanup.sh deliberately leaves backups/ .sql.gz alone — one owner of the retention policy.

search.heading: Known gaps
search.text: Gap Where Neither backup.sh nor restore.sh is shipped by a workflow (only sheet-sync.sh is); a change on main does not reach the droplet until copied by hand .github/workflows/ship-sync-schedule.yml Without BACKUP GPG RECIPIENT FILE the upload proceeds unencrypted with only a log warning; without BACKUP HEALTHCHECK URL that warning is never seen deploy/backup.sh --verify checks R2 only when R2 ACCESS KEY ID is set; otherwise it passes on the local dump alone deploy/backup.sh verify block monthly/ is pruned by the script at 400 days while the documented lock is 365 days deploy/backup.sh KEEP REMOTE MONTHLY DAYS ; DEPLOY.md The prune also deletes objects at the bucket root older than 30 days, a leftover from before the folders existed deploy/backup.sh

Everything MahekOne knows lives in one database on one server. This page explains how that database is protected: what is copied, how often, where the copies go, how long they are kept, how anybody knows the copies actually work, and what is not covered. The developer tab has the exact commands.

search.heading: Two kinds of backup, doing two different jobs
search.text: Server snapshot Database backup What it copies The whole machine — operating system, configuration, the database files The data — every table, as a file that can be loaded into any database Who makes it DigitalOcean, once a day MahekOne's own backup script, four times a day Good for "The server is gone" "Somebody deleted the wrong thing", "a bad update damaged records", "the disk failed" Where it is kept DigitalOcean On the server and in Cloudflare R2, a separate company's storage Encrypted DigitalOcean's own Yes — before it leaves the server A machine snapshot restores everything to how it was, including the mistake you want to undo, and it is at best a day old. A data backup can be restored on its own, onto any machine, from any point in the last thirteen months. Having both means losing the server and losing a record are two different, survivable problems.

search.heading: What is protected
search.text: - The MahekOne database — customers, orders, bills, payments, calls, the field team's visits and attendance, HR, the ERP, settings, credentials set on screens, and every photograph that is stored in the database (the default — see Storage). - Every other database on the same server — today that is the public website's enquiries and applications — copied alongside, each in its own file.

search.heading: How often, and how far back
search.text: Copy When (India time) Kept on the server Kept in R2 Nightly 02:15, after the night's sync and rebuild have finished 7 days 30 days Daytime 08:15, 14:15, 20:15 2 days 7 days Monthly The nightly copy taken in the early hours of the 2nd of each month — about 13 months So: - A disk failure loses at most about six working hours — the gap between two daytime copies. - A mistake noticed a week later can be undone from a nightly copy. - A mistake noticed months later still has a monthly copy to go back to.

search.heading: Encryption
search.text: Every copy sent to R2 is encrypted on the server before it leaves , with a key whose private half is held only by people , in a password manager — never on the server. Anybody who broke into the server, or into the R2 account, would find copies they cannot read. Losing the private key loses every offsite copy. The private key and its passphrase are the only way to read an R2 copy. If both are lost, every offsite backup is unreadable for ever — that is the price of an intruder not being able to read them either. Keep them in the password manager, and make sure a second person can reach them.

search.heading: How anybody knows the backups work
search.text: An untested backup is a belief. Three things check them: 1. Every run checks its own file — big enough to be the real database, and a complete, uncorrupted file — before calling itself done. 2. Every Monday at 04:00 the newest copy is restored into a scratch database and compared, table by table, with the live one. If any key table comes back with noticeably fewer rows than live, the check fails. It also confirms a nightly copy reached R2 in the last 36 hours. 3. An outside alert (a free healthchecks.io check) is pinged at the start and end of every run. It emails two people when a run fails — and, just as important, when no run arrives at all , which is the failure a log file can never report. There is also a ten-minute restore drill to do by hand before relying on any of this (on the developer tab): take a backup, create a throwaway table, restore, and check the table has gone.

search.heading: Protection against deleting the backups themselves
search.text: The credential the server uses to upload copies can also delete them — the script tidies old copies with it. So anybody who got onto the server could, in principle, delete the database and every backup in one sitting. The answer is a bucket lock in Cloudflare: each folder of copies is locked for as long as it is meant to be kept, and a locked copy cannot be deleted or overwritten by anybody, the server included, until it reaches that age.

search.heading: Restoring
search.text: Restoring replaces the whole database with the chosen copy. It is done by somebody with access to the server, the app is stopped while it happens, and the script will not proceed until the operator types the word replace . Anything written between the copy and the restore is lost, which is why restores are planned for the evening. Situation What to restore from A mistake noticed today The newest daytime copy on the server — no key needed A mistake noticed this month A nightly copy from R2 — needs the private key A mistake noticed months ago A monthly copy from R2 — needs the private key The server is gone Rebuild from the DigitalOcean snapshot, or a fresh server plus the newest R2 copy

search.heading: What is not covered
search.text: - The server's own settings file ( /opt/mahekone/.env — database password, cron secret, R2 credentials, service account key). Only the DigitalOcean snapshot holds it. Keep a copy in the password manager. - Photographs stored in an R2 attachments bucket , if that has been switched on. Those live in their own bucket, not in the database backup. - The spreadsheets the team types into — they are Google's, and MahekOne only reads them. - The APK download on the server — every release is archived in R2 separately. - Anything written since the last copy.

search.heading: One-time setup — checklist
search.text: These four steps are done once. Until each is done, the protection it adds is missing; the backup script itself warns in its log when the first is missing. Step What it gives How to tell it is done Create the encryption key on a personal machine, store the private half and passphrase in the password manager, put only the public half on the server Offsite copies an intruder cannot read The R2 file names end in .gpg ; the log no longer says "the R2 copy is NOT encrypted" Create the healthchecks.io check (every 6 hours, 1 hour grace, two email recipients) and give the server its ping address An email when a backup fails or does not happen The check shows pings from both a daytime run and the Monday verify Add a bucket lock rule per folder ( daily/ 30 days, intraday/ 7 days, monthly/ 365 days) and matching lifecycle rules Backups the server cannot delete Visible in Cloudflare under the bucket's settings Run a daytime backup and a verify by hand, then the restore drill Proof, rather than belief The verify lists every table ok ; the drill's throwaway table is gone after restore

search.heading: Where the code and the intent disagree today
search.text: - The verify step skips the offsite check if R2 is not configured. On a server with no R2 credentials the Monday verify passes on the local copy alone, and the only warning is a line in the backup log ( deploy/backup.sh , verify mode). - Old copies are deleted by the script by age only. The intended protection against deleting backups is the bucket lock, which is a manual setup step; until it is set, the server's credential can delete any copy.

Configuration in MahekOne is three stores with three different rules: settings ( app settings , declared in one registry, cached, audited with values), credentials ( app secrets , read only by the request about to spend them, audited without values), and the process environment (read at start-up or per request from process.env ). This page covers the code behind each, how to add a setting without breaking the server build, and every environment variable the code actually reads.

search.heading: Map of the code

search.heading: A setting is a registry entry
search.text: SETTINGS is one long array of these. getConfig() layers whatever is stored in app settings over defaultConfig() , so a key never written simply reads its default — adding a setting needs no migration. The cache is per process. invalidateConfig() clears the cache only in the process that wrote. The production app is one container, so a save is visible on the next read; a job running in another process (a npm run jobs on a laptop) sees it within 30 seconds of its own cache.

search.heading: Validation and consistency
search.text: Every write validates against the definition first — type, bounds, options, nullability: Then the whole configuration is checked for contradictions between keys (a stage threshold against the window that feeds it, a strong-health threshold at or below the watch one, a recording limit above Sarvam's ceiling with the fallback off, and so on). updateSettings refuses a page save only if it introduces a problem that was not already present; updateSetting (single key) saves and returns the problems as warnings.

search.heading: Who may write which key
search.text: requireConfigWriteFor(keys) in src/lib/actions/crm.ts asks for config.write and then, for anybody who is not the platform administrator, that every key's page (via placeSetting ) is owned by an app they hold at manager or admin level. Platform-page keys and keys marked adminOnly in PRESENTATION are the platform administrator's alone, and the platform administrator must have confirmed their password within .

search.heading: Settings on the handset
search.text: mbos. keys reach the handset on every pull as part of the configuration channel, so a change made at a desk lands on phones on their next sync. The handset reads them from its local cache; a key that is not sent falls back silently to the handset's default, which is why mbos-wire.test.ts pins the spelling of the keys both sides share.

search.heading: Adding a setting
search.text: Add the registry entry. In SETTINGS in src/lib/config/registry.ts : key, type, category, label, a description a manager can act on, a default, and min / max or options . Never type the number into an engine. Add the Config type entry — or the server build breaks. Config is a hand-written type further down the same file. A key in SETTINGS with no entry in Config type-checks in most places and fails next build where getConfig()["your.key"] is read. Place it on a page. Make sure a rule in settings-placement.ts (or a tab in PRESENTATION ) places it. settings-placement.test.ts fails the build on a setting that sits on no page — a setting nobody can find cannot be changed. Add a consistency rule if it pairs with another key. In checkConsistency , with a sentence that names both keys. Read it through the engine's config type. Pass it into the pure engine as an argument; read getConfig() in the service. Changing a shipped default. Write a migration that updates the stored value only where updated by id is null , so a value somebody chose is left alone (see 0042 day boundary midnight , 0120 check in is a gate ). A setting whose default is null breaks every integration test unless it is marked nullable and written through storedSettingValue — app settings.value is jsonb NOT NULL .

search.heading: The list is closed
search.text: Only names in SECRET NAMES can be stored, and each maps to the environment variable it falls back to:

search.heading: Reading one
search.text: readSecret is the only function that selects a value. The console row wins; the environment is the fallback. It is deliberately not cached , so a rotated key stops working at once. Screens call secretStatuses() , which selects last4 and the source ( console , environment or unset ) and never the value: Writes go through setSecretAction / clearSecretAction (platform administrator only), which audit secret.set / secret.clear with the name and never the value. The one exception: the Ola Maps key. A map tile key must reach whoever draws tiles, so the Ola key is handed to the browser as a prop by the page that draws the map, and to a bound handset in its sync payload. The mitigations are a domain restriction in Ola's console for the web key and a separate key with a spend cap for the handset. See Integrations.

search.heading: .env.local and .env.prod.local
search.text: - .env.local is the laptop's own environment: DATABASE URL to your local Postgres, and whatever optional keys you are testing. npm run jobs , db:seed and the other tsx scripts pass --env-file=.env.local . - .env.prod.local holds a DATABASE URL pointing at production through an SSH tunnel ( ssh -N -L 5433:127.0.0.1:5432 deploy@one.mahekindia.com ). npm run jobs:prod loads only that file. - npm run jobs:prod:sheets loads .env.local first (for the Google credentials) and .env.prod.local second , so production's DATABASE URL wins. The order of the two files is the whole safety. With the files reversed, .env.local 's DATABASE URL wins, and a "production" job writes to your local database and reports success. A prod job also runs your checkout's code, not what is deployed — make sure your tree is current with main first.

Almost every number that shapes how MahekOne behaves — how many days before a customer counts as inactive, how far a salesman may stand from a shop and still check in, how long a payment promise keeps a customer off the calling list, how big a photograph may be — is a setting . Settings are changed from a screen, take effect within about half a minute, and every change is recorded with who made it and what it was before. Nothing about a setting needs a developer or a redeploy. This page explains the three kinds of configuration MahekOne has, who can change which, and why credentials are kept apart from everything else. The developer tab has the code.

search.heading: The three kinds of configuration
search.text: Kind Examples Who changes it Where Settings Call Log windows, collection stages, check-in radius, attachment size limit, the working day Managers who may change configuration, for the apps they hold; platform administrators for everything Admin Console → Settings, one page per app Credentials (keys) The WhatsApp (Wati) key, the sign-in code (MiniMoth) key, dictation keys, the maps keys, the website enquiry secret Platform administrators only Admin Console → Integrations (and the Voice and Maps sections) Server environment Where the database is, the Google service account, the backup bucket, the cron secret Whoever holds shell access to the droplet The file /opt/mahekone/.env on the droplet The first two are on screens because a deployment that nobody has shell access to must still be able to be tuned and connected. An environment variable is a door somebody else has to open; a setting is a decision the business can make for itself. Only the things the app needs before it can even start — where its database is — have to live in the environment.

search.heading: Settings
search.text: Nothing business-critical is a constant. If a manager might one day want to change a number, it is a setting, not a value typed into the code. Each setting has a label, a description, a default, and limits (a minimum and maximum, or a list of allowed values). A value outside those limits is refused when it is saved.

search.heading: Where they are changed
search.text: Admin Console → Settings has one page per app that has something to configure: Page What it decides Who can open it besides a platform administrator Platform Sign-in, the working day, file uploads, and the other settings every app shares Nobody — these decide things for everybody Telecaller CRM The call queue, collections, buying cycles Managers holding the CRM Lead funnel The gates a lead must pass, the reason lists, lead behaviour on the handset Managers holding the CRM or the Sales Dashboard Sales and field app Attendance, tracking, visits, orders, expenses, salesman targets Managers holding the Sales Dashboard or the Salesman App Accounts How money is recorded and confirmed; how price lists are read and discounted Managers holding Accounts HRMS Check-in, overtime, payroll deductions, performance points Managers holding HRMS ERP Production tolerances, whether the ERP takes orders, its alerts Managers holding the ERP Hire Which models evaluate candidates, how sure they must be, the AI budget Managers holding Hire Reports How the owner's figures are measured Holders of the Founder Command Centre Voice and AI Dictation and the assistants Managers holding the CRM An app with nothing to configure has no page , rather than a page that says so.

search.heading: What happens when you save
search.text: Saving a settings page. - A page saves as one change. Related settings — three escalation thresholds, a set of age bands — are written together or not at all, so the system never briefly describes something nobody agreed to. - Contradictions are refused only if the save introduces them. If two settings already disagree, saving a fix to one half is allowed; refusing would trap whoever is trying to repair it. - Every change is audited with the value before and after, and who made it. - There is no restart. Values are read through a short cache, so a change is in force within about thirty seconds everywhere. A setting nobody has ever changed uses its default . Adding a new setting therefore needs no data change — it simply starts at its default on every deployment.

search.heading: Credentials
search.text: Credentials — the keys MahekOne uses to call outside services — are kept in a separate place from settings, and treated differently in four ways: 1. They are never shown. A screen shows only the last four characters, so two keys can be told apart and nobody can read one off a screen. 2. The audit records that a key changed, never what to. Settings are audited with their before and after values; a key logged that way would sit readable in an audit log nobody prunes. 3. They are not exported. Settings can be exported and are rendered on screens; keys are read only by the request about to use them. 4. Only platform administrators can set or clear them. A key kept with the ordinary settings would be readable in four places — the screen, the export, the audit log and the database — and one of those is a log that keeps everything for ever. Keeping keys in their own place, read only at the moment they are spent, removes three of the four.

search.heading: The console wins over the server environment
search.text: Most keys can be set either on the Integrations screen or as a variable in the server's environment file. Where both are set, the one set on the screen wins ; where only the environment has one, that one is used. So a deployment that already had its keys in the environment needed no change, and a key can be rotated from a screen without anybody logging into the server. A key is stored as written. There is nowhere to keep an encryption key that MahekOne can read and a database backup cannot, so credentials set on the screen are stored as typed. Backups are encrypted before they leave the server (see Backups), but if a database dump ever leaves your hands unencrypted, rotate every key at its provider . The Integrations screen says this too.

search.heading: What each credential switches on
search.text: Credential What it enables Without it WhatsApp (Wati) Sending templates and reading replies; also the delivery webhook address Nothing is sent through the API; copy-and-confirm still works Sign-in codes (MiniMoth) One-time codes to the phone Codes fall back to a Wati template if one is named, or are not offered; passwords still work Dictation (Sarvam, OpenAI) The microphone on prose fields No microphone is drawn Maps (Ola, up to five keys) Street maps, snapping trails to roads, geocoding Map screens say there is no key rather than drawing a blank Website enquiries secret The public website forwarding enquiries Enquiries from the website are refused See Integrations for each service in detail.

search.heading: The server environment
search.text: A handful of things cannot be settings, because the app needs them before it can read the database, or because they belong to the machine rather than the business: - Where the database is — the only one the app refuses to start without. - The Google service account that reads the team's spreadsheets. - The cron secret that the server's own scheduler presents to run syncs and nightly jobs. - The backup bucket and its encryption key file . - The file store for photographs, when they move out of the database. - The sign-in signing secret for the handset. These live in /opt/mahekone/.env on the droplet, readable only by the deploy user. A missing one does not crash the app: the feature that needs it goes quiet and says so (the sync reports "not configured", the microphone is not drawn, reset mail is written to the log). That is deliberate — but it also means a mistyped name is silent, which is why a test compares the example file's names against the names the code reads.

search.heading: Who can do what
search.text: - Changing settings needs config.write and a grant in an app that owns the page; Platform settings are for platform administrators only. - Setting or clearing credentials is for platform administrators only. - Server environment changes need shell access to the droplet.

search.heading: Where the code and the intent disagree today
search.text: - The time zone setting is not read by the database queries. decides the business date in the app, but every day window written in SQL uses a fixed Asia/Kolkata constant. Changing the setting would make the two disagree. - A credential is declared that nothing uses. The list of known credentials includes an SMS provider key ( msg91.authKey ) that can be set on the screen, but no code reads it; sign-in codes go through MiniMoth ( src/lib/secrets.ts ). - Some settings are shown but never read. For example describes how long removed attachments are kept, but no code reads it (see Storage).

Production is one DigitalOcean droplet in Bangalore (1 GiB / 1 vCPU / 25 GiB, Ubuntu 24.04) running three containers under Docker Compose: Caddy (TLS and the APK download), the app (the Next.js standalone server) and Postgres 17 . The image is built on GitHub's runners, pushed to the DigitalOcean Container Registry, and pulled by the droplet; migrations run from the runner through an SSH tunnel. Only Caddy publishes a port. The whole thing costs a few dollars a month, and the database sitting next to the app is most of why screens are fast. This page is the operator's reference: the topology, what one deploy does step by step, the secrets it needs (by name), first-time provisioning, day-to-day operations, rollback, and the traps that have actually bitten. The source of truth is DEPLOY.md in the repository root; this page follows it and the files it describes.

search.heading: Topology
search.text: What runs where. File What it is Dockerfile Three stages on node:24-alpine : npm ci , next build (standalone), a runner as uid 1001 with only .next/standalone , .next/static and public deploy/docker-compose.yml caddy , app , postgres on one bridge network; volumes pgdata , caddy data , caddy config Caddyfile {$DOMAIN} : compression, /downloads/ served from /srv/downloads , everything else to app:3000 with 300 s timeouts, immutable cache on / next/static/ deploy/bootstrap.sh One-time host preparation (swap, sysctls, Docker, firewall, unattended upgrades) deploy/restart.sh docker compose up -d --remove-orphans and wait for every container to report healthy deploy/sheet-sync.sh What the crontab calls for the sync cycles — see Sheets and jobs deploy/backup.sh , deploy/restore.sh See Backups deploy/cleanup.sh Weekly tidy: old APK copies, old images by name, the journal, the sync log

search.heading: The containers
search.text: Service Notes caddy Only container with published ports. Mounts ./downloads read-only for the handset APK and its mbos.json manifest. Obtains the certificate for DOMAIN on first start. app NODE OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=320 . env file: .env . Healthcheck fetches /login every 30 s. Waits for Postgres to be healthy. postgres TZ and PGTZ set to Asia/Kolkata (the code still names the zone everywhere — see Architecture). Tuned for 1 GiB: shared buffers=128MB , work mem=8MB , max connections=20 , jit=off , pg stat statements loaded, slow-query log at 500 ms. Port bound to 127.0.0.1 only. The database password never leaves the droplet and the deploy runner. Postgres listens on loopback, and the firewall ( ufw ) allows only 22, 80 and 443.

search.heading: One deploy, end to end
search.text: push to main → production. Test. npm ci , npx tsc --noEmit , npx eslint src , npm test (the pure suites). The full CI — migrations from scratch, integration journeys, the handset's lint, types and engine tests, the link crawl — runs separately in ci.yml on every PR. Build on GitHub's runners. The droplet never builds: at 1 GiB it cannot. DATABASE URL is set to a deliberately unresolvable host during next build , because src/db/index.ts throws without one and the build must never reach a real database. GIT SHA becomes NEXT DEPLOYMENT ID , so a browser holding the previous build's chunks is told to reload rather than failing on a missing file. Refuse a stale commit. concurrency: deploy-production with cancel-in-progress usually handles two quick merges, but a run that has already built may still reach the deploy job. It asks GitHub where main is now and skips if it has moved past — deploying would put an older commit back. Migrate through a tunnel. deploy:db is db:deploy (migrations via scripts/migrate-deploy.mjs ), then catalogue:deploy (the idempotent product import), then hire:deploy . It runs on the runner against 127.0.0.1:5433 , forwarded to the droplet's loopback Postgres. Migrations run before the new image starts, so new code never meets an old schema; old code briefly meets the new one, which is why migrations here are additive. Swap the image. IMAGE= in /opt/mahekone/.env is rewritten to the new tag, docker compose pull app , then restart.sh brings everything up and waits for healthy. A few seconds of downtime; a save in flight sees an error and is retried. Prove it is serving. https://$DOMAIN/login must return 200 within five minutes or the run fails, naming the log command. Prune the registry — last. See The registry quota.

search.heading: First-time provisioning
search.text: Create the droplet. Regular 1 GiB, BLR1, Ubuntu 24.04, daily backups and monitoring on, your SSH key added, a reserved IP attached. Create the registry ( mahekone ) and an R2 bucket for backups with an S3 API token. Prepare the host. Then create the deploy user in the docker group, copy the authorised keys, and give it /opt/mahekone . Copy the files. Fill in .env . Generate the Postgres password with openssl rand , and put the same value in the POSTGRES PASSWORD GitHub secret. DNS before the first start. An A record for the domain to the reserved IP, propagated ( dig +short one.mahekindia.com ) before Caddy starts — Let's Encrypt verifies by connecting, and a failed challenge costs a rate-limit wait. Start Postgres alone, then deploy. Then push to main or run Deploy by hand. Install the schedules. bash /opt/mahekone/backup.sh --install-cron , and add the sheet-sync.sh lines to the deploy user's crontab by hand (see below).

search.heading: Rolling back
search.text: A rollback is naming an earlier image tag that is still in the registry or on the droplet: The registry keeps the newest three tags plus latest and whatever production is on; the droplet keeps its newest three images. A rollback across a migration is a different thing — restore the dump instead (see Backups).

search.heading: Running a job by hand against production
search.text: Two traps in one command. jobs:prod:sheets loads .env.local first and .env.prod.local second so production's DATABASE URL wins; reversed, it writes to your laptop's database and reports success. And either form runs your checkout's code against production — be on current main .

search.heading: The droplet's crontab
search.text: The host clock is UTC . backup.sh --install-cron writes its own three lines and leaves the rest alone; the sync lines are added by hand. UTC IST Command :07 , :37 every hour — sheet-sync.sh cycle :22 every hour — sheet-sync.sh hourly 20:13 01:43 sheet-sync.sh nightly 20:45 02:15 backup.sh 02:45 , 08:45 , 14:45 08:15, 14:15, 20:15 backup.sh --intraday 22:30 Sunday 04:00 Monday backup.sh --verify 04:30 on the 1st 10:00 on the 1st sheet-sync.sh monthly sheet-sync.sh itself is shipped by the Ship sync schedule workflow whenever it changes on main (it is syntax-checked on the runner and again on the droplet before it replaces the old one). The crontab lines are not shipped — check with crontab -l after adding a new cycle.

search.heading: The registry quota
search.text: The free registry holds 500 MB and an image is about 130 MB. When it is full, the push fails with denied: quota exceeded , the build job goes red, and deploy is skipped — which reads as nothing having happened rather than as a storage problem. - The prune job runs after the deploy: keep latest , the live tag (read from the droplet's .env ) and the newest three; delete the rest; start a garbage collection. - It runs last because DigitalOcean will not start collecting until every write-scoped push token has expired; collecting right before this run's own push produced 401 Unauthorized . The build job instead waits (up to 10 minutes) for any collection still running. - Registry prune ( registry-prune.yml ) is the same thing by hand, with a keep input. If a deploy has already failed on the quota, clear space by hand — the prune cannot unblock the run it is inside:

search.heading: Protecting main
search.text: Every push to main deploys, so main moves only through a pull request with green CI. The rules are a repository ruleset defined in .github/rulesets/main.json and applied with scripts/apply-branch-ruleset.sh : no direct or force pushes, PR only, all required CI jobs green, review threads resolved, admin bypass through a PR only. Renaming or adding a CI job means editing the ruleset in the same PR — src/lib/branch-ruleset.test.ts fails when the two disagree.

search.heading: Cost and capacity
search.text: Item Notes Droplet The 1 GiB plan plus daily backups. Resize to 2 GiB (RAM and CPU only — a disk resize cannot be undone) when swap sits above about 500 MB, the memory alert fires often, or the projection or nightly start timing out. Registry Free tier, 500 MB — the binding constraint, see above. R2 Backups and the APK archive; pennies at this volume. What you give up No preview deployments, a few seconds of downtime per deploy, rollback in a minute rather than a click, and nobody else watching the machine (unattended security upgrades reboot it at 03:30 when needed).

The field salesman's app (MBOS, mbos-app/ , Android package in.mahek.mbos ) reaches phones two ways. Native changes — a new native module, a permission, an Expo SDK bump, the API base — ship as a signed APK , built and published by the MBOS APK GitHub workflow and installed by sideloading. JavaScript changes — screens, copy, engine rules — ship over the air with eas update , and a handset picks them up in the background without a reinstall. Push notifications ride on Expo's push service through Firebase, and need two credentials set once. There is no store, no staged rollout and no rollback for a sideloaded APK, so a release is a decision somebody makes by pressing a button — never a push trigger, and never a file copied up from a laptop.

search.heading: Map of the release machinery

search.heading: Releasing an APK
search.text: MBOS APK workflow, publish: true. Bump both version numbers first. In mbos-app/app.json , raise expo.version and expo.android.versionCode — in the same PR as the change or in a PR of its own, merged before you run the workflow. versionCode is the integer Android compares to decide an install is an upgrade, and what the update nudge compares; the version string is for people and is what Admin Console → Handsets shows. Left unbumped, every phone reports the same build and nobody can tell whether a fix has reached a salesman. Try it without publishing. The APK is attached to the run (Artifacts) and goes in front of nobody. Publish. Optionally set the reference build. tells Admin Console → Handsets which build every phone should be on; empty, it uses the newest version any phone has reported.

search.heading: What the workflow refuses
search.text: Check Why it refuses api base not https://… , or ending in / It is baked into the bundle at build time ( EXPO PUBLIC API BASE ) and cannot be changed afterwards — a wrong one is a broken binary, not a wrong setting MBOS KEYSTORE STORE PASSWORD empty Without the release key gradle would sign with a debug key; Android treats that as a different app, and every salesman would have to uninstall — losing anything unsynced — to update Signer certificate does not match the committed keystore Same consequence, and invisible on a clean test phone. Checked with apksigner verify --print-certs , not keytool -printcert -jarfile , which finds no JAR signature on a modern APK and silently verifies nothing Live /downloads/mbos.apk hash differs from the build The publish did not land; nothing anybody downloads is this build

search.heading: Where it is published, and why twice
search.text: Destination Name Purpose R2 ( R2 DOWNLOADS BUCKET ) mbos- - .apk and mbos.apk The versioned archive; outlives any droplet Droplet /opt/mahekone/downloads/ mbos.apk , mbos.json What people are given a link to: https://one.mahekindia.com/downloads/mbos.apk . Caddy serves it off local disk; nothing serves /downloads from R2 Files are copied to a dot-prefixed temporary name and mv 'd into place, so a download never sees half a file. deploy/cleanup.sh keeps mbos.apk plus one older local copy.

It skips the signature check, the versioned archive and the record of what shipped. Local gradlew assembleRelease is for trying a change on your own phone. A hand-copied release has happened once; the workflow exists so it does not happen again.

search.heading: The update nudge
search.text: The handset fetches ${API BASE}/downloads/mbos.json (cache-busted, six-second timeout) on open and hands it to a pure rule. It is a static file rather than an API route on purpose: the moment a salesman most needs to update is the moment his build is too old to sign in. Anything missing, malformed, non-https, or not strictly newer answers current and draws nothing. The app cannot install an APK itself; the card hands the link to the browser.

search.heading: Over-the-air updates
search.text: expo-updates is enabled in app.json against the EAS project in extra.eas.projectId , with the channel pinned in updates.requestHeaders["expo-channel-name"] = "production" . Builds are made by gradle in the workflow, not by eas build , so nothing else stamps a channel in — without the pinned header a handset asks for updates on no channel and receives none. Rule Why runtimeVersion uses the fingerprint policy It hashes the native project, so a native change produces a new runtime whether or not anybody remembered to bump the version — and an update is only delivered to builds of the same runtime. An update reaches only builds of its runtime A phone on an older APK keeps the JavaScript it has until it installs a newer APK. To patch an old build, publish against that build's runtime (read it out of the APK) — see the team's notes. Native changes never go over the air A new native module, a permission, an SDK bump, and EXPO PUBLIC API BASE are always an APK. An update never delays a launch fallbackToCacheTimeout: 0 , checkAutomatically: ON LOAD : the app opens on what it has, downloads behind it, and runs the new bundle next time. It never reloads under somebody's half-filled form. The Sync screen says which bundle is running "Running the build that was installed" or the update's id, so "the fix is not on my phone" and "the fix does not work" can be told apart.

search.heading: Push notifications
search.text: Every notification is written to the in-app bell whatever happens to the push. Push only adds the lock-screen banner. From a notification to a phone. Settings: , , , .

search.heading: Turning push on, once
search.text: Create a Firebase project and register the Android app. Package name exactly in.mahek.mbos . Download google-services.json . Give it to the APK build. Paste the whole file as the repository secret MBOS GOOGLE SERVICES JSON . The workflow writes it and names it in app.json for that build only; its log says "Firebase configured for this build". Let Expo send through it. Generate a Firebase service-account key and upload it to the EAS project's credentials as the FCM V1 Google Service Account ( npx eas-cli@latest credentials -p android , or expo.dev → Credentials). Without this the handsets get tokens and Expo refuses to deliver. Ship an APK. Firebase is native, so this cannot go over the air. Check. mbos devices.push token fills in as salesmen open the new build, and the handset's Profile says push is on. The handset's own punch-out reminder switches itself off once the office's notification takes over.

search.heading: Changing the release process safely
search.text: Keep the signature check. Any change to signing must keep the apksigner comparison against the committed keystore. A mis-signed APK installs on a clean phone and fails only on the phones that matter. Keep publishing atomic. Copy to a temporary name, then mv ; write mbos.json only after the APK is in place, so the nudge never points at a file that is not there yet. Never relax the api base guard. The value is compiled in. A staging build checks its own droplet's manifest for the same reason.

Every outside service has one client file that owns the HTTP calls, reads its credential through readSecret (console first, environment second — see Configuration), and returns a result type rather than throwing. Each also has a readiness question the screens ask before drawing the feature. No SDKs are used where a fetch will do: Google, Wati, MiniMoth, Resend, Ola and S3 are all plain HTTP; only dictation's OpenAI path goes through the AI SDK.

search.heading: Sending
search.text: src/lib/wati.ts talks to Wati's v3 API with a Bearer token and decides nothing — whether a message may go (the founder's switch, an approved template, the number, the weekly limit ) is whatsapp-service.ts 's question, asked before the client is called. The founder's switch is the newest row of whatsapp service events (no row means off), read on every send rather than cached. whatsapp.activate is the capability that flips it.

search.heading: Receiving
search.text: Wati's webhook settings take a URL and nothing else, so the path segment is the credential, derived from the API key: A Wati delivery or reply event. Rotating the key rotates the address — update it in Wati's webhook settings at the same time. Hourly jobs whatsapp-receipts and wa-reply-media catch up on anything a webhook missed.

search.heading: MiniMoth and sign-in codes
search.text: Order Provider Condition 1 MiniMoth minimoth.apiKey held, and not an mm test key while NODE ENV=production 2 Wati authentication template named, a Wati key held, and the template approved in Wati — None available: false with a reason; the login page shows passwords only MiniMoth generates and verifies the code ( sendMiniMothOtp , verifyMiniMothOtp ); MahekOne's auth otps row records that one was sent and the MiniMoth id. The destination is the HRMS personal mobile of the linked employee. Limits are settings: , , . otpAvailability never throws — the container's health check is the login page, so a settings read failing during a migration must cost the code option, never the sign-in screen.

search.heading: Ola Maps
search.text: Five named credentials rather than one list, spent in order. With one key held, calls go straight through; with several, a quota refusal is recorded and the next key is used, and the spent one is skipped for hours. Use Where Key travels to Live and Territory maps (tiles, style, glyphs) src/app/sales/live/page.tsx , src/app/sales/territory/page.tsx → ola-maps.tsx The browser , as a prop from liveOlaKey() — restrict it to the domain in Ola's console Handset map Sync payload to a bound device The phone — use a separate key with a spend cap; Ola offers no package restriction Snap-to-Road road-snap-service.ts , asked once per selected salesman per day by /api/sales/live/snap-trail Server only Geocoding, places, directions, distance ola-geocode-service.ts and siblings, geocode-customers job Server only The key is never put in the style URL on the handset — requests are signed at the HTTP layer so offline map packs are stored key-less and survive a key rotation.

search.heading: Resend
search.text: Returns { delivered: true } , { reason: "not configured" } (written to the server log) or { reason: "failed", detail } . Swapping provider means editing the delivery function only. APP URL makes the reset link absolute behind a tunnel.

search.heading: Sarvam and OpenAI (dictation and writing)
search.text: Rule Detail Hearing Sarvam ( saaras ) for recordings up to 30 s, run as transcribe and translate in parallel; longer or failed recordings go to OpenAI when allows — and always when no Sarvam key is held Writing writing-model.ts tries OpenAI then Sarvam; a permanent refusal (no credit, revoked key) moves to the next rather than surfacing Readiness No key → no microphone; canRefine false → Tighten/Rewrite omitted Audio Never stored; route handlers (not actions) because two minutes of audio exceeds the 1 MB action body limit Doors /api/dictate/ (session) and /api/mbos/dictate/ (device token) share src/lib/dictation-requests.ts , including the six refusal sentences Settings: , , .

search.heading: Google service account
search.text: A self-signed JWT (RS256, spreadsheets.readonly scope) is exchanged for an hour-long token, cached in module scope with a minute of headroom. GOOGLE SA PRIVATE KEY is stored with literal \n ; the client converts them, and "invalid JWT signature" from Google almost always means that conversion did not happen. The service account must hold Viewer on each workbook.

search.heading: Expo push
search.text: Tokens are registered by the handset at POST /api/mbos/push-token onto mbos devices.push token . Sends go to https://exp.host/--/api/v2/push/send in chunks of 100; collectPushReceipts reads receipts hourly and clears tokens Expo reports as DeviceNotRegistered . See Handset release for the Firebase setup.

search.heading: The public website
search.text: /api/public/enquiries compares the presented secret with readSecret("enquiries.ingestSecret") in constant time and refuses anything else; duplicates are reported rather than created twice. It is server-to-server only — the secret never reaches a browser on either side.

search.heading: Adding an integration
search.text: Declare the credential. Add a name to SECRET NAMES with its environment fallback, and to .env.production.example (commented) so env-names.test.ts agrees. One client file. Plain fetch with a timeout, readSecret per call (no caching of keys), a result type rather than a throw. A readiness function the screen asks first. Missing key → the feature is not drawn, or says it is not set up. Never draw a control that fails when pressed. Inbound webhooks authenticate before parsing. A derived path token or a shared secret, compared in constant time; cap the body size; answer 404 to a wrong token. A row on the Integrations screen. Via secret-credential-row.tsx , so a deploy nobody has shell access to can still be connected.
